Focus and Dilution: The Multi-stage Learning Process of Attention

Zheng-An Chen Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University.    Pengxiao Lin Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Affiliation: Institute of Natural Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University.    Zhi-Qin John Xu Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Affiliation: Institute of Natural Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Affiliation: MOE-LSC, Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Affiliation: Shanghai Seres Information Technology Co., Ltd, Shanghai 200040, China. Correspondence to: xuzhiqin@sjtu.edu.cn    Tao Luo Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Affiliation: Institute of Natural Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Affiliation: MOE-LSC, Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Abstract

Transformer-based models have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of domains, yet our understanding of their training dynamics remains limited. In this work, we identify a recurrent focus–dilution cycle in attention learning and provide a rigorous explanation in a one-layer Transformer setting for Markovian data via gradient-flow analysis. Using stage-wise linearization around critical points, we show that a single focus–dilution cycle can be decomposed into a sequence of distinct stages. First, embedding and projection rapidly condense to a rank-one structure, while attention parameters remain effectively frozen. Then, the attention parameters begin to increase, inducing a frequency-driven focus toward high-frequency tokens. As attention continues to evolve, it generates next-order perturbations in embeddings, leading to a mass-redistribution mechanism that progressively dilutes this focus. Finally, small asymmetries among low-frequency tokens lift a degenerate critical point, opening new embedding directions and initiating the next cycle. Experiments on synthetic Markovian data as well as WikiText and TinyStories corroborate the predicted stages and cyclical dynamics.

Keywords: 
Attention mechanism, Training dynamics, Multi-stage analysis, Condensation
††affiliationnotice: Equal contribution.

1 Introduction

Transformer models (Vaswani et al., 2017) have become the dominant architecture for sequence modeling. While their approximation power is now well understood in a variety of regimes (Pérez et al., 2019; Yun et al., 2020a; Yun et al., 2020b), we still lack a mechanistic theory for how attention itself evolves during training. Most existing analyses gain tractability by introducing additional technical condition, such as reparameterizations (Zhang et al., 2024a) or proxy dynamics (Tarzanagh et al., 2023), which may obscure the native coupling among embeddings, projection, and attention. Moreover, recent work suggests that Transformer training often undergoes multiple stages (Chang et al., 2024; Varre et al., 2025), and that attention can shift from highly concentrated to more diffuse patterns (Tian et al., 2024). These observations point to a need for a dynamical picture that remains faithful to the coupled dynamics and can explain both attention amplification and its subsequent dissipation.

In this work, we combine theory and experiments to show that attention can be understood as a cyclical learning process. Within each cycle, attention first amplifies a frequency-driven preference over tokens (focus), and then gradually weakens this preference as the embedding structure adapts (dilution). We identify the dynamical origin of each stage and explain how the interaction between embeddings and attention progressively decomposes the learning problem.

To keep the analysis tractable while preserving essential sequential structure, we study population gradient flow for a one-layer Transformer trained by cross-entropy on Markov data (Chang et al., 2024; Makkuva et al., 2024; Makkuva et al., 2025). Our explanation is stage-wise and built on linearizations around critical points. Under small initialization, the trajectory is first governed by the linearization near the origin, which forces a rank-one condensation of the embedding and projection components, consistent with the condensation phenomenon in Chen & Luo (2025). We further observed that the condensed direction is explicitly determined by the stationary distribution. In contrast, the attention parameters remain small in this initial stage because the leading-order driving term for (WQ,WK)(W_{Q},W_{K}) vanishes at the origin.

After condensation, the trajectory follows the same low-rank ray until it reaches a second critical point. We show that this point is generically a saddle: the Jacobian admits a local block decomposition into (i) a contracting embedding/output subsystem and (ii) an attention subsystem with a single unstable mode. Consequently, once the trajectory enters this neighborhood, (WQ,WK)(W_{Q},W_{K}) align with the unstable eigendirection and grow exponentially, and attention acquires a bias toward high-frequency tokens, initiating the focus phase.

Going beyond the focus phase requires a more refined description than the local saddle analysis. Once (WQ,WK)(W_{Q},W_{K}) align with the unstable direction, dynamics enters to a rank-one invariant manifold and induces a closed reduced system. This reduced flow exposes a mass-redistribution mechanism in the embeddings. As the attention amplitude evolves, it generates next-order perturbations, causing the embeddings of the main token and the remaining tokens to move in opposite directions. As a result, the earlier high-frequency focus is gradually weakened, leading to an attention dilution phase.

Finally, the model must learn new embedding directions that distinguish low-frequency tokens. However, we show that the training dynamics become trapped at a degenerate critical point on the rank-one manifold, where the driving forces vanish and no new directions can emerge. To model realistic asymmetries and eliminate degeneration, we introduce a small symmetry-breaking perturbation among low-frequency tokens and analyze the resulting bifurcation of critical points. This mechanism explains how new embedding directions are unlocked, thereby initiating the next focus–dilution cycle. Experiments on synthetic Markovian data as well as WikiText and TinyStories corroborate the predicted stages and cyclical dynamics.

Our contributions.
  1. 1.

    We identify a focus–dilution cycle in the training dynamics of attention and introduce a minimal tractable setting that captures this phenomenon.

  2. 2.

    We develop a stage-wise analysis based on linearization at critical points that explains the different stages within single cycle.

  3. 3.

    We empirically validate the predicted stages and transitions, demonstrating that the focus–dilution cycle persists on synthetic Markov data as well as realistic data.

Definition 2.1 (Markovian data).

Let P∈ℝd×dP\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be row-stochastic. For each i∈[N]i\in[N], sample xi,1∼Unif⁡(𝒱)x_{i,1}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{V}) and xi,j∼Pxi,j−1x_{i,j}\sim P_{x_{i,j-1}} for j=2,…,s+1j=2,\dots,s+1. Set Xi=(xi,1,…,xi,s)X_{i}=(x_{i,1},\dots,x_{i,s}) and yi=xi,s+1y_{i}=x_{i,s+1}.

To model one high-frequency token together with a group of low-frequency tokens that may exhibit mild heterogeneity, we consider a stationary distribution of the form π⊺​(δ):=(π1,…,πd)\pi^{\intercal}(\delta):=(\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{d}) with

πi=1−π1d−1+ci​δ,∀ 2≤i≤d,\pi_{i}=\frac{1-\pi_{1}}{d-1}+c_{i}\delta,\quad\forall\ 2\leq i\leq d, (1)

The first term describes two-group setting, one high-frequency token and the rest symmetrical low-frequency tokens. The second term is an O⁡(δ)O(\delta) perturbation that breaks symmetry within the low-frequency group. P=λ​I+(1−λ)​𝟏​π⊺,0<λ<1,P=\lambda I+(1-\lambda)\mathbf{1}\pi^{\intercal},\qquad 0<\lambda<1, (2)

3 Theoretical results

3.1 Idea: stage-wise linearization around saddle points

Under small initialization, attention training often exhibits a multi-stage pattern: the trajectory spends a long time near a low-dimensional structure and then abruptly departs in a new direction. We explain this behavior via a stage-wise analysis around successive critical points. At each stage, the parameters enter a neighborhood of a saddle point where the gradient flow is well-approximated by its linearization. The linearized dynamics exposes (i) stable directions that keep the trajectory confined to a low-dimensional manifold, and (ii) unstable directions that eventually dominate and trigger the transition to the next stage.

Concretely, we consider the gradient flow θ˙=−∇ℒ​(θ)\dot{\theta}=-\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta). Let θ∗\theta_{*} be a critical point, and define Δ​θ:=θ−θ∗\Delta\theta:=\theta-\theta_{*}. A Taylor expansion yields

dd​t​Δ​θ=−∇2ℒ​(θ∗)​Δ​θ+higher-order terms.\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Delta\theta=-\nabla^{2}\mathcal{L}(\theta_{*})\,\Delta\theta+\text{higher-order terms}.

The next lemma characterizes the linearization in which the nonlinear flow is governed by the linearized system, and formalizes the alignment with the most unstable direction.

Lemma 3.1 (Linearization near a saddle point).

Let θ˙=F⁡(θ)\dot{\theta}=F(\theta) be an ODE with F∈C2F\in C^{2}, and let θ∗\theta_{*} satisfy F⁡(θ∗)=0F(\theta_{*})=0. Let J:=D​F​(θ∗)J:=DF(\theta_{*}) and assume there exist r>0r>0 and L>0L>0 such that for all ‖Δ​θ‖≤r\|\Delta\theta\|\leq r,

‖F⁡(θ∗+Δ​θ)−J​Δ​θ‖≤L​‖Δ​θ‖2.\|F(\theta_{*}+\Delta\theta)-J\Delta\theta\|\leq L\|\Delta\theta\|^{2}. (6)

Let θ⁡(t)\theta(t) be the solution with ‖Δ​θ​(0)‖=ε≤r/2\|\Delta\theta(0)\|=\varepsilon\leq r/2, and Δ~​θ​(t):=eJ​t​Δ​θ​(0)\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t):=\mathrm{e}^{Jt}\Delta\theta(0) be the solution of the linearized system Δ~˙​θ=J​Δ~​θ\dot{\tilde{\Delta}}\theta=J\tilde{\Delta}\theta. Define μ:=sup{ℜ⁡(λ):λ∈σ⁡(J)}\mu:=\sup\{\Re(\lambda):\lambda\in\sigma(J)\}. Then for all tt such that ‖Δ~​θ​(t)‖≤r/2\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|\leq r/2,

‖Δ​θ​(t)−Δ~​θ​(t)‖≤C​ε2​e2​μ​t\|\Delta\theta(t)-\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|\;\leq\;C\,\varepsilon^{2}\,\mathrm{e}^{2\mu t} (7)

for some constant C=C⁡(J,L)C=C(J,L). In particular, if μ>0\mu>0, then the nonlinear dynamics is well-approximated by the linearized dynamics up to times t=Θ⁡(log⁡(1/ε))t=\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)).

Moreover, suppose JJ is symmetric and has a simple eigenvalue μ>0\mu>0 with eigenvector vuv_{u} and a spectral gap ρ>0\rho>0 in the sense that λ≤μ−ρ\lambda\leq\mu-\rho for all λ∈σ⁡(J)∖{μ}\lambda\in\sigma(J)\setminus\{\mu\}. Then for any initialization with ⟨Δ​θ​(0),vu⟩≠0\langle\Delta\theta(0),v_{u}\rangle\neq 0,

Δ​θ​(t)‖Δ​θ​(t)‖→±vu‖vu‖\frac{\Delta\theta(t)}{\|\Delta\theta(t)\|}\to\pm\frac{v_{u}}{\|v_{u}\|} (8)

for any sequence t=t⁡(ε)t=t(\varepsilon) with t⁡(ε)→∞t(\varepsilon)\rightarrow\infty and ε​eμ​t​(ε)→0\varepsilon\mathrm{e}^{\mu t(\varepsilon)}\rightarrow 0.

At initialization, each entry of every parameter matrix is sampled i.i.d. from 𝒩⁡(0,ε2)\mathcal{N}(0,\varepsilon^{2}) with ε≪1\varepsilon\ll 1. Thus θ⁡(0)\theta(0) lies in an 𝒪⁡(ε)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)-neighborhood of the origin, which is a critical point of the gradient flow. By Lemma 3.1, the dynamics in the early time window of length Θ⁡(log⁡(1/ε))\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)) is governed by the linearization at θ=0\theta=0. A key consequence is that the linearized system admits a single unstable direction, so trajectories rapidly align with a rank-one direction. In our setting, this direction is not arbitrary: it is explicitly pinned down by the stationary distribution π\pi of the underlying token Markov chain.

The origin is a critical point and

∂ℒ∂M|θ=0=−π​(π−1d​𝟏)⊺,∂ℒ∂Φ|θ=0=0.\left.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}\right|_{\theta=0}=-\pi\left(\pi-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}\right)^{\intercal},\qquad\left.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}\right|_{\theta=0}=0. (9)

The effective dynamics near θ=0\theta=0 is

d​Δ​W0d​t=−∂ℒ∂M|θ=0​Δ​W1⊺,\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\Delta W_{0}}{\mathrm{d}t}=-\left.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}\right|_{\theta=0}\Delta W_{1}^{\intercal}, d​Δ​W1d​t=−Δ​W0⊺​∂ℒ∂M|θ=0\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\Delta W_{1}}{\mathrm{d}t}=-\Delta W_{0}^{\intercal}\left.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}\right|_{\theta=0} (10)

Consequently, there exist a vector α1\alpha_{1} such that the following limit holds as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 at t=𝚯⁡(log⁡1ε)t=\bm{\Theta}(\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}):

W0‖W0‖→π‖π‖α1⊺,W1‖W1‖→α1π⊺−1d​𝟏⊺‖π⊺−1d​𝟏⊺‖.\displaystyle\frac{W_{0}}{\|W_{0}\|}\rightarrow\frac{\pi}{\|\pi\|}\alpha_{1}^{\intercal},\quad\frac{W_{1}}{\|W_{1}\|}\rightarrow\alpha_{1}\frac{\pi^{\intercal}-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}^{\intercal}}{\|\pi^{\intercal}-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}^{\intercal}\|}. (11)

Theorem 3.2 characterizes the first stage of training dynamics in our model. Although it is rephrased from Thm. 2 in (Chen & Luo, 2025), we emphasize a more concrete interpretation relevant to data. As a result, (W0,W1)(W_{0},W_{1}) rapidly condense onto a π\pi-driven rank-one structure within time T1=Θ⁡(log⁡(1/ε))T_{1}=\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)). In contrast, the attention block (WQ,WK)(W_{Q},W_{K}) stays 𝒪⁡(ε)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon) throughout this stage because the linear term in its dynamics vanishes at the origin, i.e., ∂ℒ/∂Φ|θ=0=0\left.\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\Phi\right|_{\theta=0}=0.

3.2 Focus of Attention

After initial condensation stage, outer parameters (W0,W1)(W_{0},W_{1}) rapidly become approximately rank-one, while the attention parameters (WQ,WK)(W_{Q},W_{K}) remain O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon). Empirically, the trajectory then stays close to the rank-one condensation ray where the outer parameters evolve along the same direction until it enters a neighborhood of a second critical point.

Proposition 3.3 (Existence of a second critical point on the condensation ray).

Assume π1>π2=⋯=πd\pi_{1}>\pi_{2}=\cdots=\pi_{d}. Then there exists κ1>0\kappa_{1}>0 such that the parameter tuple θc1\theta_{c}^{1}

W0=κ1π‖π‖α1⊺,W1=κ1α1π⊺−1d​𝟏⊺‖π−1d​𝟏‖,WQ,WK=0,W_{0}=\kappa_{1}\frac{\pi}{\|\pi\|}\alpha_{1}^{\intercal},W_{1}=\kappa_{1}\alpha_{1}\frac{\pi^{\intercal}-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}^{\intercal}}{\big\|\pi-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}\big\|},W_{Q},W_{K}=0, (12)

satisfies ℙi=π⊺\mathbb{P}_{i}=\pi^{\intercal} for all ii and ∂ℒ∂M|θ=θc1=0\left.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}\right|_{\theta=\theta_{c}^{1}}=0. Moreover, θc1\theta_{c}^{1} is a critical point of the full gradient flow.

The key point is that θc1\theta_{c}^{1} is typically a saddle: the (W0,W1)(W_{0},W_{1})-subsystem is contracting (or neutrally stable due to symmetry), while the (WQ,WK)(W_{Q},W_{K})-subsystem contains an unstable mode.

Proposition 3.4 (Linearized dynamics and its unique unstable direction).

At critical point θc1\theta_{c}^{1} defined in Prop. 3.3, the linearization of the gradient flow admits the block form

dd​t​(Δ​W0Δ​W1Δ​WQΔ​WK)=(Jout00Jatt)​(Δ​W0Δ​W1Δ​WQΔ​WK)\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\begin{pmatrix}\Delta W_{0}\\ \Delta W_{1}\\ \Delta W_{Q}\\ \Delta W_{K}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}J_{\mathrm{out}}&0\\ 0&J_{\mathrm{att}}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Delta W_{0}\\ \Delta W_{1}\\ \Delta W_{Q}\\ \Delta W_{K}\end{pmatrix} (13)

where JoutJ_{\mathrm{out}} is negative semi-definite and JattJ_{\mathrm{att}} is positive semi-definite. It indicates that the current dynamics are dominated by the attention subsystem. In particular, the attention block satisfies the explicit closed system

dd​tΔWQ=cα1α1⊺ΔWK,dd​tΔWK=cα1α1⊺ΔWQ,\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Delta W_{Q}=c\,\alpha_{1}\alpha_{1}^{\intercal}\Delta W_{K},\qquad\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Delta W_{K}=c\,\alpha_{1}\alpha_{1}^{\intercal}\Delta W_{Q}, (14)

where c=λ​κ14​‖π‖Var⁡(π)4‖π−1d​𝟏‖​‖π‖3>0c=\lambda\kappa_{1}^{4}\frac{\|\pi\|_{\operatorname{Var}(\pi)}^{4}}{\big\|\pi-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}\big\|\,\|\pi\|^{3}}>0. Therefore the attention block has an exponentially unstable mode.

By Lemma 3.1, once the trajectory enters an O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon)-neighborhood of θc1\theta_{c}^{1}, the dynamics is governed by the linearization for a duration Θ⁡(log⁡(1/ε))\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)). It implies that the attention parameters (WQ,WK)(W_{Q},W_{K}) converge into the direction depending on the condensation direction. As a result, the attention structure prioritizes tokens that appear frequently in the steady-state distribution, indicating that the attention mechanism has become specific.

Theorem 3.5 (High frequency token bias).

Suppose the trajectory enters an O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon)-neighborhood of θc1\theta_{c}^{1}. Within the linearization neighborhood of Lemma 3.1, there exists a unit vector α~1∈ℝm\tilde{\alpha}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} such that, for generic small initialization of (WQ,WK)(W_{Q},W_{K}),

WQ​(t)‖WQ​(t)‖→α1​α~1⊺,WK​(t)‖WK​(t)‖→α1​α~1⊺.\frac{W_{Q}(t)}{\|W_{Q}(t)\|}\ \rightarrow\ \alpha_{1}\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\intercal},\qquad\frac{W_{K}(t)}{\|W_{K}(t)\|}\ \rightarrow\ \alpha_{1}\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\intercal}. (15)

Consequently, along the unstable ray WQ=WK=κ​α1​α~1⊺W_{Q}=W_{K}=\kappa\,\alpha_{1}\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\intercal}, the attention score matrix satisfies

Φ‖Φ‖=W0​WQ​WK⊺​W0⊺‖W0​WQ​WK⊺​W0⊺‖=π​π⊺.\frac{\Phi}{\|\Phi\|}=\frac{W_{0}W_{Q}W_{K}^{\intercal}W_{0}^{\intercal}}{\|W_{0}W_{Q}W_{K}^{\intercal}W_{0}^{\intercal}\|}\ =\ \pi\pi^{\intercal}. (16)

Then for each i∈[d]i\in[d] the attention distribution exhibits a high-frequency bias:

limκ→∞𝔸i​(W0,W1,κ​α1​α~1⊺,κ​α1​α~1⊺)=e1⊺.\lim_{\kappa\to\infty}\mathbb{A}_{i}\!\left(W_{0},W_{1},\kappa\alpha_{1}\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\intercal},\kappa\alpha_{1}\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\intercal}\right)=e_{1}^{\intercal}. (17)

3.3 Dilution of Attention

Sec. 3.2 shows that the second critical point θc1\theta_{c}^{1} is a saddle whose unique unstable direction lies in the attention subsystem: after a transient of length Θ⁡(log⁡(1/ε))\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)), the attention parameters become approximately rank-1 and aligned while the outer parameters remain close to their initial values on the condensation ray. In this subsection, we stay in the same neighborhood of θc1\theta_{c}^{1} but go beyond linearization: Conditioned on the rank-1 manifold, we resolve the next-order perturbations in embeddings induced by the evolution of attention. This refinement reveals a redistribution effect in the embeddings that gradually undermines the previously formed focus, leading to the dilution phase.

Motivated by the alignment result in Sec. 3.2, we model the post-transient phase by the rank-one parametrization

W0=γ⁡(t)​α1⊺,\displaystyle W_{0}=\gamma(t)\,\alpha_{1}^{\intercal}, W1=α1β(t)⊺,\displaystyle W_{1}=\alpha_{1}\,\beta(t)^{\intercal},\qquad (18)
WQ=λQ​(t)​α1​α~1⊺,\displaystyle W_{Q}=\lambda_{Q}(t)\,\alpha_{1}\,\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\intercal}, WK=λK​(t)​α1​α~1⊺,\displaystyle W_{K}=\lambda_{K}(t)\,\alpha_{1}\,\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\intercal},

where γ⁡(t),β⁡(t)∈ℝd\gamma(t),\beta(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and λQ​(t),λK​(t)∈ℝ\lambda_{Q}(t),\lambda_{K}(t)\in\mathbb{R}. At the entry time t0t_{0} of this phase,

γ⁡(t0)=κ1​π‖π‖,\displaystyle\gamma(t_{0})=\kappa_{1}\frac{\pi}{\|\pi\|}, β⁡(t0)=κ1​π−1d​𝟏‖π−1d​𝟏‖,\displaystyle\beta(t_{0})=\kappa_{1}\frac{\pi-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}}{\big\|\pi-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}\big\|}, (19)
λQ​(t0)\displaystyle\lambda_{Q}(t_{0}) =λK​(t0)=o⁡(1).\displaystyle=\lambda_{K}(t_{0})=o(1).

For notational convenience, we also define the attention amplitude η⁡(t):=λQ​(t)​λK​(t)\eta(t):=\lambda_{Q}(t)\lambda_{K}(t) which is the only combination that enters the reduced dynamics below.

Proposition 3.6 (Invariant rank-one manifold).

Assume π1>π2=⋯=πd\pi_{1}>\pi_{2}=\cdots=\pi_{d}. Define

𝒲:={θ​satisfying (18) for some ​(γ,β,λQ,λK)}.\mathcal{W}:=\Big\{\theta\ \text{satisfying \eqref{eq:rank1_manifold_param_rewrite} for some }(\gamma,\beta,\lambda_{Q},\lambda_{K})\Big\}.

If (W0,W1,WQ,WK)∈𝒲(W_{0},W_{1},W_{Q},W_{K})\in\mathcal{W} at time t0t_{0}, then the gradient flow (4) remains in 𝒲\mathcal{W} for all t≥t0t\geq t_{0}. Moreover, if γ2​(t0)=⋯=γd​(t0)\gamma_{2}(t_{0})=\dots=\gamma_{d}(t_{0}) and β2​(t0)=⋯=βd​(t0)\beta_{2}(t_{0})=\dots=\beta_{d}(t_{0}), it will be preserved for any t≥t0t\geq t_{0}.

Restricting the gradient flow to 𝒲\mathcal{W} yields a closed system in (γ,β,η)(\gamma,\beta,\eta):

γ˙\displaystyle\dot{\gamma} =−∂ℒ∂M​β−η⁡(∂ℒ∂Φ+(∂ℒ∂Φ)⊺)​γ,\displaystyle=-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}\,\beta-\eta\Big(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}+\Big(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}\Big)^{\intercal}\Big)\gamma, (20)
β˙\displaystyle\dot{\beta} =−(∂ℒ∂M)⊺γ,η˙=−2ηγ⊺∂ℒ∂Φγ.\displaystyle=-\Big(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}\Big)^{\intercal}\gamma,\quad\dot{\eta}=-2\eta\,\gamma^{\intercal}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}\gamma.

By Proposition 3.6, it suffices to track two-group coordinates

γ1,γ2=⋯=γ|𝒱|:=γi≠1,\displaystyle\gamma_{1},\quad\gamma_{2}=\cdots=\gamma_{|\mathcal{V}|}:=\gamma_{i\neq 1},
β1,β2=⋯=β|𝒱|:=βi≠1,\displaystyle\beta_{1},\quad\beta_{2}=\cdots=\beta_{|\mathcal{V}|}:=\beta_{i\neq 1},

and denote Δ​γ:=γ1−γi≠1\Delta\gamma:=\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{i\neq 1}, Δ​β:=β1−βi≠1\Delta\beta:=\beta_{1}-\beta_{i\neq 1}. Intuitively, this reduces the post-alignment dynamics to an effective two-group system (token 1 versus all others). Importantly, we are still analyzing the flow near the same critical point θc1\theta_{c}^{1}; the difference from Sec. 3.2 is that we can keep the attention direction fixed and resolve the next-order feedback that governs redistribution on the rank-one manifold.

Theorem 3.7 (Mass redistribution).

Consider the linearization of reduced dynamics (20) on 𝒲\mathcal{W} at critical point corresponding to θc1\theta_{c}^{1}. There exists c>0c>0 such that

(1−π1)​γ1​(t)−(d−1)​π1​γi≠1​(t)∝exp⁡(c​t).(1-\pi_{1})\gamma_{1}(t)-(d-1)\pi_{1}\gamma_{i\neq 1}(t)\propto\exp(ct). (21)

Consequently, γ1​(t)\gamma_{1}(t) and γi≠1​(t)\gamma_{i\neq 1}(t) cannot move in the same direction: a weighted contrast between high-frequency token and the remaining tokens is exponentially amplified.

Theorem 3.7 explains the mechanism behind the dilution phase. After alignment, the attention direction is essentially fixed, and the attention amplitude η⁡(t)\eta(t) feeds back into γ˙\dot{\gamma} through the η⁡(∂ℒ/∂Φ)​γ\eta(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\Phi)\gamma term in (20). The redistribution effect forces a growing separation between γ1\gamma_{1} and γi≠1\gamma_{i\neq 1}, so the embedding mass cannot remain concentrated along π\pi.

Therefore, the logit difference that causes high-frequency bias gradually weakens: the attention weights corresponding to low-frequency tokens are no longer concentrated on high-frequency tokens. This marks a shift from focus to dilution.

3.4 Emergence of a new direction via data asymmetry

In Sec. 3.3, the dynamics collapses onto a rank-one invariant manifold, effectively reducing learning to a “token 1 vs. all others” two-group system. Further learning requires separating low-frequency states, which demands growth of embeddings along directions that distinguish low-frequency tokens.

However, for perfectly symmetric data among low-frequency tokens, the rank-one manifold may contain a degenerate critical point where both driving forces vanish: ∂ℒ/∂M=0\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial M=0 and ∂ℒ/∂Φ=0\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\Phi=0. Crucially, the degeneracy is not only tangential, but also transverse. As a consequence, linearization does not generate a mechanism that pushes the trajectory away from the rank-one manifold.

Proposition 3.8 (Degenerate critical point).

Assume perfect symmetry among low-frequency tokens. On the rank-one invariant manifold 𝒲\mathcal{W} (Proposition 3.6), there exists a critical point, which is a neutrally stable equilibrium for the linearized dynamics, such that ∂ℒ∂M=0\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}=0 and ∂ℒ∂Φ=0\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}=0.

The solution to remove degeneracy is to introduce perturbations that breaks the symmetry. In practice, low-frequency tokens rarely have identical frequencies. To model a minimal asymmetry while keeping calculations simple, we focus on d=3d=3 and perturb the stationary distribution by a small parameter δ\delta:

π⊺=(π1,1−π12,1−π12)⇒π~⊺=(π1,1−π12+δ,1−π12−δ)\pi^{\intercal}=(\pi_{1},\tfrac{1-\pi_{1}}{2},\tfrac{1-\pi_{1}}{2})\ \Rightarrow\ \tilde{\pi}^{\intercal}=(\pi_{1},\tfrac{1-\pi_{1}}{2}+\delta,\tfrac{1-\pi_{1}}{2}-\delta)

We study stationary points of the perturbed gradient field −∇θℒ​(θ,δ)=0-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta,\delta)=0 near the degenerate critical point. After shifting coordinates so that θ=0\theta=0 corresponds to the degenerate critical point, a formal expansion takes the form

−∇ℒ​(θ,δ)=J0​θ+δ​f1+h.o.t.,-\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta,\delta)=J_{0}\theta+\delta f_{1}+\text{h.o.t.}, (22)

where J0=−∇θ2ℒJ_{0}=-\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\mathcal{L} at δ=0\delta=0.

If J0J_{0} were invertible, the implicit function theorem would apply, and we could directly obtain the solution θ⁡(δ)\theta(\delta). Unfortunately, due to symmetry, J0J_{0} is degenerate, so we use the standard Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction. Let QK=(k1,…,kdK)Q_{K}=(k_{1},\dots,k_{d_{K}}) and QR=(q1,…,qdR)Q_{R}=(q_{1},\dots,q_{d_{R}}) be orthonormal bases for the kernel and range subspaces of J0J_{0}:

ℝp=Ker⁡(J0)⊕Ran⁡(J0),θ=QK​x+QR​y,\mathbb{R}^{p}=\operatorname{Ker}(J_{0})\oplus\operatorname{Ran}(J_{0}),\qquad\theta=Q_{K}x+Q_{R}y,

where pp is the parameter dimension. Projecting the stationarity condition onto the range and kernel yields the equivalent system

−QR⊺∇ℒ(θ,δ)=0,−QK⊺∇ℒ(θ,δ)=0.-Q_{R}^{\intercal}\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta,\delta)=0,\quad-Q_{K}^{\intercal}\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta,\delta)=0. (23)

The range equation can be solved by the implicit function theorem since QR⊺​J0​QRQ_{R}^{\intercal}J_{0}Q_{R} is invertible, yielding a smooth map y=ζ⁡(x,δ)y=\zeta(x,\delta). Substituting back into the kernel equation produces a reduced low-dimensional problem in xx whose solutions describe nearby stationary points.

The key effect of the perturbation is that it splits the previously flat transverse directions. A genuinely transverse positive eigenvalue of order Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta) appears, while tangential instability is at most 𝒪⁡(δ2)\mathcal{O}(\delta^{2}). This fast transverse instability is what drives the trajectory away from the rank-one manifold and seeds a new embedding direction.

Theorem 3.9 (Asymmetry lifts degeneracy and induces a new direction).

Consider the perturbed stationary distribution with parameter δ\delta above. There exists a point θ⁡(δ)\theta(\delta) near the degenerate critical point such that

‖∇θℒ​(θ⁡(δ),δ)‖=O⁡(δ3).\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta(\delta),\delta)\|=O(\delta^{3}). (24)

Moreover, the Hessian at θ⁡(δ)\theta(\delta) exhibits two distinct scales:

1. Slow tangential instability. Any positive eigenvalues created from the previously degenerate directions are at most O⁡(δ2)O(\delta^{2}).

2. Fast normal instability. Under mild condition, in directions transverse to the rank-one manifold, there exists a positive eigenvalue of order Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta).

Theorem 3.9 shows that any generic low-frequency asymmetry lifts this degeneracy and produces a fast transverse unstable mode of size Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta). Once the trajectory enters the neighborhood of θ⁡(δ)\theta(\delta), this transverse instability drives it away from the degenerate rank-one configuration and enables the emergence of a genuinely new embedding direction, allowing the model to further differentiate low-frequency tokens beyond the two-group description.

4 Empirical evidence

In this section, leveraging the simplified transformer model, we analyze the training behavior on Markovian data and empirically validate the theoretical derivation describing the transition of attention from focus to dilution. In parallel, we evaluate the model on real-world WikiText corpora and on the TinyStories corpus, which exhibits basic linguistic structure, to assess whether our observations generalize to the training dynamics of large-scale language models in realistic settings.

4.1 Synthetic Experiments

We construct synthetic datasets using four distinct transition matrices PP, designed to share a common stationary distribution π=(0.75,0.19,0.05,0.01)\pi=(0.75,0.19,0.05,0.01). To reveal the low-rank structure of parameters caused by condensation, we measured the cosine similarity between neuronal input weights for analysis (Chen & Luo, 2025; Xu et al., 2025b).

Additionally, we visualize the embedding trajectory evolution by applying Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to the concatenated embedding snapshots across all steps (Lorch, 2016; Antognini & Sohl-Dickstein, 2018). Detailed experimental setups are provided in Appendix E. The overall evolution of the training dynamics is visualized in Fig. 2. We identify four distinct stages during the training process. In the following, we provide a detailed analysis of each stage to demonstrate the consistency between our experimental observations and theoretical results.

Stage I: Initial Condensation

Our theoretical analysis predicts that during this stage, the outer layers W0,W1W_{0},W_{1} evolve from an initialized full-rank state to a low-rank structure, while the inner attention parameters remain largely invariant. This is depicted by Fig. 2(A), which demonstrates that the outer weights rapidly evolve into rank-1, whereas the WQ,WKW_{Q},W_{K} maintain the high-rank nature of their initialization. Simultaneously, Fig. 2(B1) illustrates that the embeddings of all tokens evolve towards a uniform direction, further validating our theoretical analysis.

Stage II: Growth of Attention

During this stage, the outer parameters remain largely invariant, while WQW_{Q} and WKW_{K} transition into a condensed state. This phase coincides with a significant drop in training loss, marking the evolution of parameters from the origin to the next critical point. According to our theory, the attention mechanism evolves such that high-frequency tokens are gradually focused by the remaining tokens. This phenomenon is clearly visualized in Fig. 2(C).

Stage III: Dilution of Attention

In Stage III, although the parameters remain confined to the rank-1 manifold (evidenced by the unchanged condensation heatmap in Fig. 2(A)), Fig. 2(B2) reveals that all tokens, except for token 0, exhibit a retraction trajectory. This implies that while the training dynamics are strictly constrained within the low-rank manifold, the model begins to differentiate between tokens. As shown in Fig. 2(C, D), low-frequency tokens pay less attention to high-frequency token in this phase, accompanied by a significant drop in the embedding norms of low-frequency tokens. Consequently, outer parameters of the network revert to an unstable state.

Stage IV: Emergence of New Direction

In Stage IV, the accumulated instability drives the model to escape the constraints of the rank-1 manifold, initiated by the growth of new directions in the outer layers. This transition is clearly observable in Fig. 2(B3). To further quantify this, in Fig. 2(D3), we project the embeddings of low-frequency tokens (W0[1:]W_{0}[1:]) onto the direction orthogonal to token 0 (denoted as W0​[0]⟂W_{0}[0]_{\perp}) and calculate the projection norms. The results indicate that, for the first time, the remaining token embeddings significantly deviate from the direction of token 0.

After Stage IV: Subsequent Training Dynamics

Fig. 2(D) further illustrates the later stages of the training process, revealing a distinct periodicity in the embedding norms. Specifically, the focus and dilution pattern repeats recursively: as the network proceeds to learn Token 1, the remaining tokens (2–3) undergo the same retraction and regrowth process, continuing sequentially until training concludes. We hypothesize that after Stage IV, the model has effectively converged on Token 0. Consequently, the system evolves into a sub-dynamic regime governed by Tokens 1–3. In this reduced state, the parameter dynamics can be re-analyzed within our original theoretical framework.

4.2 Real-world Experiments

Experimental Results.

We validate the correctness of our theorem on two real-world datasets: WikiText (Merity et al., 2016) and TinyStories (Eldan & Li, 2023). We employ the same simplified Transformer architecture and maintain hyperparameter settings consistent with the synthetic data experiments. To investigate the “focus-and-dilution” characteristics of the attention mechanism, we track the top-three most frequent tokens alongside three randomly sampled medium-frequency tokens (frequency >10%>10\%) from the training set.

As illustrated in the figure, across both WikiText and TinyStories, the attention mechanism exhibits a consistent pattern: it initially prioritizes high-frequency tokens (e.g., “the”, “a”, and whitespace) before subsequently losing this focus—a process we term “dilution.” Concurrently, by monitoring the embedding evolution of these selected tokens, we observe a distinct “retraction” phenomenon. Notably, due to the high variance in batch composition inherent to the 1-epoch training regime on real-world corpora, we occasionally observe this retraction even in the most frequent tokens.

Validity of the Markov Approximation.

Existing studies (Chang & Bergen, 2022; Chang et al., 2024) indicate a curriculum in Transformer learning, starting from 1-gram to n-gram statistics. Our analysis of attention patterns in TinyStories supports this: distinct tokens gradually shift from uniform attention to self-attention. This behavior indicates that the model functions as a pseudo-2-gram model during early training phases, despite the non-Markovian nature of real text. These observations indirectly validate our experimental design, confirming that our synthetic Markov data acts as a suitable proxy for understanding real-world training dynamics.

5 Conclusion

This work advances the theoretical understanding of transformer training dynamics by providing a mechanistic account of how attention evolves. We identify a recurring focus–dilution cycle and develop a stage-wise gradient-flow framework that characterizes rank-one condensation, saddle-to-saddle transitions, and the impact of symmetry breaking, offering a rigorous basis for phenomena often reported empirically. While the formal analysis is derived in a restricted setting, the same qualitative signatures appear on real corpora, suggesting the framework remains a useful lens for interpreting early-stage attention dynamics beyond the idealized regime.

Limitation

This paper provides a minimal analytical framework for studying the coupled evolution of embeddings and attention, and identifies the focus–dilution cycle as a concrete mechanism. Experiments on synthetic data and small-scale natural language data provide preliminary support for this mechanism. Owing to the limitations of the theoretical framework, our analysis mainly focuses on the training dynamics of single-layer attention, and thus does not yet capture the effects of layer interactions or multi-head structure. Extending the analysis to multi-layer and multi-head architectures, and studying how common components such as LayerNorm affect the dynamics, are important directions for future work.

Impact Statement

This paper aims to advance the theoretical understanding of transformer training dynamics by providing a mechanistic analysis of attention evolution. While improved understanding of learning dynamics may inform future model design and training practices, we do not foresee any direct negative ethical or societal consequences arising specifically from this work.

Appendix A Related Works

Training dynamics of attention and multi-stage analysis

Given the scale of modern models and the complexity of optimizers, studying the training dynamics of attention remains a challenging problem. A common practice is to introduce various simplifications to the research object, such as constructing task-specific synthetic data, utilizing reparameterization or simplified model and optimization function (Sheen et al., 2024; Kim & Suzuki, 2024; Varre et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024a; Wu et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a; Vasudeva et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). Among these, (Lu et al., 2021) establishes key dynamical identities using a controllable text classification task where sentences consist of a “topic word” plus random noise. (Snell et al., 2021) suggests that models first capture word co-occurrence before adjusting attention to focus on relevant tokens. (Li et al., 2023) examines the dynamical effects of fixing specific attention components within a topic-word task framework. Following these previous works, (Tian et al., 2024) proposed a novel mathematical framework for analyzing the joint dynamics of MLP and attention blocks, successfully explaining the sparsity of attention score matrices. (Zucchet et al., 2025) also discussed the emergence of sparse attention and the timing of training dynamics. Furthermore, (Yang et al., 2024) provides a clear and rigorous discussion of the two-stage training dynamics under classifiable text tasks. Similarly, (Chen & Luo, 2025) offers a more rigorous proof of dynamical separation in more general scenarios. Regarding multi-stage analysis, (Xu et al., 2025a) analyzes LoRA’s cross-stage dynamics, while (Wang & Ma, 2023) provides a full-process characterization of two-layer ReLU networks across four distinct training phases, from initialization to convergence. (Varre et al., 2025) shows in an analyzable in-context n-gram setting that lower-order sub-n-gram solutions are near-stationary points, explaining the plateau-to-drop training dynamics as Transformers gradually learn to retrieve longer contexts. However, the aforementioned literature either relies on data settings that deviate significantly from real-world scenarios or requires overly stringent analytical conditions.

Transformers on Markov chains

A significant body of influential work employs Markov chains to understand how Transformers, as probabilistic models, learn continuous linguistic data. (Chang et al., 2024) discovers that LLM learning can be summarized as “early n-gram learning followed by the gradual refinement of low-probability (tail) n-gram predictions.” (Bietti et al., 2023) analyzes the formation mechanism of induction heads using Markov-like data. (Rajaraman et al., 2024) investigates the impact of tokenization on Markovian data, proving that appropriate tokenization assists Transformers in modeling Markov processes. Additionally, (Makkuva et al., 2024) and (Makkuva et al., 2025) explore training dynamics and convergence analysis specifically under Markovian data settings.

Small initialization

The initialization of a neural network significantly affects its learning outcomes (Arora et al., 2019; Williams et al., 2019; Mei et al., 2018; Jacot et al., 2018; Rotskoff & Vanden-Eijnden, 2018; Zhang et al., 2020). Small initialization is a common setting investigated in the study of neural network optimization dynamics, which contrasts with the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) perspective prevalent in infinitely wide networks. For linear models, (Ji & Telgarsky, 2019) theoretically establish results regarding matrix alignment. For nonlinear models, (Zhou et al., 2022) found that small initialization similarly promotes parameter condensation, thereby reducing model complexity. Theoretically, (Luo et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2024b; Zhou et al., 2023; Kumar & Haupt, 2024) have further deepened the understanding of this phenomenon. A recent survey article (Xu et al., 2025b) systematically synthesizes these empirical and theoretical findings.

Appendix B Theoretical details in Sec. 2

B.1 Property of markov process

We will use two standard asymptotic properties of Markov chains. For the sake of completeness, we provide a detailed proof.

Proposition B.1 (Basic Markov properties).

Given the transition matrix PP in (2) and any initial distribution μ0\mu_{0}:

  1. 1.

    Convergence. The marginal distribution converges to π\pi. That is limt→∞μ0⊺​Pt=π⊺\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\mu_{0}^{\intercal}P^{\,t}=\pi^{\intercal}.

  2. 2.

    Ergodicity. Along a single trajectory, the empirical state frequencies converge to π\pi. That is lims→∞1s​∑j=1s𝟙xj=π⊺\lim_{s\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{s}\sum_{j=1}^{s}\mathbbm{1}_{x_{j}}=\pi^{\intercal}, where 𝟙xj∈ℝd\mathbbm{1}_{x_{j}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the one-hot vector of token xjx_{j}.

Proof.

Throughout, we work on the finite state space 𝒱={1,…,|𝒱|}\mathcal{V}=\{1,\dots,|\mathcal{V}|\}. By the definition of the transition matrix PP defined in (2), PP is irreducible and aperiodic with strictly positive entries. Thus, PP is ergodic. In particular, PP admits a unique stationary distribution π\pi satisfying π⊺​P=π⊺\pi^{\intercal}P=\pi^{\intercal} and πi>0\pi_{i}>0 for all ii.

1) Convergence of marginals.

Since PP is ergodic on a finite state space, it is primitive. By the Perron–Frobenius theorem, the eigenvalue 11 of PP is simple and all other eigenvalues satisfy |λ|<1|\lambda|<1. Let 𝟏∈ℝ|𝒱|\mathbf{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|} denote the all-ones vector. Because PP is row-stochastic, we have P​𝟏=𝟏P\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}; because π\pi is stationary, we have π⊺​P=π⊺\pi^{\intercal}P=\pi^{\intercal}. Define the rank-one projector

Π:=𝟏​π⊺.\Pi:=\mathbf{1}\,\pi^{\intercal}.

Then Π2=Π\Pi^{2}=\Pi, P​Π=Π​P=ΠP\Pi=\Pi P=\Pi, and we can write

P=Π+Q,where ​Q:=P−Π.P=\Pi+Q,\qquad\text{where }Q:=P-\Pi.

Note that Q​𝟏=0Q\mathbf{1}=0 and π⊺​Q=0\pi^{\intercal}Q=0. Moreover, the spectrum of QQ equals the spectrum of PP with the eigenvalue 11 removed, hence its spectral radius satisfies ρ⁡(Q)<1\rho(Q)<1. Therefore, Qt→0Q^{t}\to 0 as t→∞t\to\infty (in any matrix norm), and

Pt=(Π+Q)t=Π+Qt→t→∞Π=𝟏​π⊺.P^{t}=(\Pi+Q)^{t}=\Pi+Q^{t}\;\xrightarrow[t\to\infty]{}\;\Pi=\mathbf{1}\,\pi^{\intercal}. (25)

For any initial distribution μ0\mu_{0} (a row vector with nonnegative entries summing to 11),

μ0⊺​Pt→t→∞μ0⊺​(𝟏​π⊺)=(μ0⊺​𝟏)​π⊺=π⊺,\mu_{0}^{\intercal}P^{t}\;\xrightarrow[t\to\infty]{}\;\mu_{0}^{\intercal}(\mathbf{1}\,\pi^{\intercal})=(\mu_{0}^{\intercal}\mathbf{1})\,\pi^{\intercal}=\pi^{\intercal},

which proves the convergence claim.

2) Ergodicity of empirical frequencies.

Let (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} be the Markov chain with transition matrix PP and arbitrary initial distribution μ0\mu_{0}. Fix a reference state, say state 11, and define the (strict) return times

τ0:=0,τk+1:=inf{t>τk:Xt=1},k≥0.\tau_{0}:=0,\qquad\tau_{k+1}:=\inf\{t>\tau_{k}:\,X_{t}=1\},\qquad k\geq 0.

By irreducibility on a finite state space, the chain is positive recurrent, hence τk<∞\tau_{k}<\infty almost surely for all kk and 𝔼1​[τ1]<∞\mathbb{E}_{1}[\tau_{1}]<\infty.

For each cycle k≥0k\geq 0, define the cycle length and the state-ii visit count within the cycle:

Sk:=τk+1−τk,Rk(i):=∑t=τkτk+1−1𝟙{Xt=i}.S_{k}:=\tau_{k+1}-\tau_{k},\qquad R_{k}(i):=\sum_{t=\tau_{k}}^{\tau_{k+1}-1}\mathbbm{1}\{X_{t}=i\}.

By the strong Markov property, conditional on Xτk=1X_{\tau_{k}}=1 the post-τk\tau_{k} evolution is independent of the past, and therefore the pairs {(Sk,Rk​(i))}k≥1\{(S_{k},R_{k}(i))\}_{k\geq 1} are i.i.d. under ℙ1MC\mathbb{P}_{1}^{\text{MC}} (and also after the chain first hits state 11 when started from an arbitrary μ0\mu_{0}). Let N⁡(T):=max⁡{k:τk≤T}N(T):=\max\{k:\tau_{k}\leq T\} be the number of completed cycles up to time TT. Then for each fixed ii,

∑t=0T−1𝟙{Xt=i}=∑t=0τ1−1𝟙{Xt=i}⏟initial transient+∑k=1N⁡(T)−1Rk(i)+∑t=τN⁡(T)T−1𝟙{Xt=i}⏟remainder.\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbbm{1}\{X_{t}=i\}=\underbrace{\sum_{t=0}^{\tau_{1}-1}\mathbbm{1}\{X_{t}=i\}}_{\text{initial transient}}+\sum_{k=1}^{N(T)-1}R_{k}(i)+\underbrace{\sum_{t=\tau_{N(T)}}^{T-1}\mathbbm{1}\{X_{t}=i\}}_{\text{remainder}}. (26)

Divide by TT. The initial transient term is O⁡(1/T)O(1/T) almost surely. The remainder term is at most one cycle, hence bounded by SN⁡(T)S_{N(T)}, and thus also negligible after dividing by TT because τN⁡(T)≤T<τN⁡(T)+1\tau_{N(T)}\leq T<\tau_{N(T)+1} implies SN⁡(T)≤τN⁡(T)+1S_{N(T)}\leq\tau_{N(T)+1} and τN⁡(T)→∞\tau_{N(T)}\to\infty.

It remains to analyze the dominant sum over complete cycles. By the strong law of large numbers applied to the i.i.d. sequences {Sk}\{S_{k}\} and {Rk​(i)}\{R_{k}(i)\},

1n∑k=1nSk→𝔼1[S1]=𝔼1[τ1],1n∑k=1nRk(i)→𝔼1[R1(i)]a.s.\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}S_{k}\to\mathbb{E}_{1}[S_{1}]=\mathbb{E}_{1}[\tau_{1}],\qquad\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}R_{k}(i)\to\mathbb{E}_{1}[R_{1}(i)]\quad\text{a.s.} (27)

Moreover, by the definition of τk\tau_{k}, we know

τN⁡(T)+1=∑k=0N⁡(T)Sk≥T,τN⁡(T)=∑k=0N⁡(T)−1Sk≤T−1\tau_{N(T)+1}=\sum_{k=0}^{N(T)}S_{k}\geq T,\quad\tau_{N(T)}=\sum_{k=0}^{N(T)-1}S_{k}\leq T-1

which implies

N⁡(T)T→1𝔼1​[τ1]a.s.\frac{N(T)}{T}\to\frac{1}{\mathbb{E}_{1}[\tau_{1}]}\quad\text{a.s.}

Combining with (26) and (27), we obtain

1T∑t=0T−1𝟙{Xt=i}→T→∞a.s.𝔼1​[R1​(i)]𝔼1​[τ1].\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbbm{1}\{X_{t}=i\}\;\xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{a.s.}\;\frac{\mathbb{E}_{1}[R_{1}(i)]}{\mathbb{E}_{1}[\tau_{1}]}. (28)

Take i=1i=1, we get the right-hand side is π1\pi_{1} by the computation about expectation of first return time. Since the above proof process is independent of the choice of the reference state, by considering all possible reference states, we obtain the result. ∎

B.2 Gradient-flow dynamics

In this section, we will supplement the proof details of Proposition 2.3.

Proof.

We first derive Eq. (4), using the standard trace theorem and chain rule. Taking the total differential of the loss, we get

d​ℒ=⟨∂ℒ∂M,d​M⟩+⟨∂ℒ∂Φ,d​Φ⟩\mathrm{d}\mathcal{L}=\left\langle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M},\mathrm{d}M\right\rangle+\left\langle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi},\mathrm{d}\Phi\right\rangle (29)

Using the chain rule, we get

⟨∂ℒ∂M,d​M⟩\displaystyle\left\langle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M},\mathrm{d}M\right\rangle =⟨∂ℒ∂M,d​W0​W1+W0​d​W1⟩\displaystyle=\left\langle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M},\mathrm{d}W_{0}W_{1}+W_{0}\mathrm{d}W_{1}\right\rangle (30)
⟨∂ℒ∂Φ,d​Φ⟩\displaystyle\left\langle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi},\mathrm{d}\Phi\right\rangle =⟨∂ℒ∂Φ,d​W0​WQ​WK⊺​W0⊺+W0​d​WQ​WK⊺​W0⊺+W0​WQ​d​WK⊺​W0⊺+W0​WQ​WK⊺​d​W0⊺⟩\displaystyle=\left\langle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi},\mathrm{d}W_{0}W_{Q}W_{K}^{\intercal}W_{0}^{\intercal}+W_{0}\mathrm{d}W_{Q}W_{K}^{\intercal}W_{0}^{\intercal}+W_{0}W_{Q}\mathrm{d}W_{K}^{\intercal}W_{0}^{\intercal}+W_{0}W_{Q}W_{K}^{\intercal}\mathrm{d}W_{0}^{\intercal}\right\rangle

We derive the evolution equation for W0W_{0}, and the other derivations are similar. We collect items related to d​W0\mathrm{d}W_{0}:

⟨∂ℒ∂M,d​W0​W1⟩+⟨∂ℒ∂Φ,d​W0​WQ​WK⊺​W0⊺+W0​WQ​WK⊺​d​W0⊺⟩\displaystyle\left\langle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M},\mathrm{d}W_{0}W_{1}\right\rangle+\left\langle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi},\mathrm{d}W_{0}W_{Q}W_{K}^{\intercal}W_{0}^{\intercal}+W_{0}W_{Q}W_{K}^{\intercal}\mathrm{d}W_{0}^{\intercal}\right\rangle (31)
=tr⁡((∂ℒ∂M)⊺​d​W0​W1)+tr⁡((∂ℒ∂Φ)⊺​(d​W0​WQ​WK⊺​W0⊺+W0​WQ​WK⊺​d​W0⊺))\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}\left(\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}\right)^{\intercal}\mathrm{d}W_{0}W_{1}\right)+\operatorname{tr}\left(\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}\right)^{\intercal}\left(\mathrm{d}W_{0}W_{Q}W_{K}^{\intercal}W_{0}^{\intercal}+W_{0}W_{Q}W_{K}^{\intercal}\mathrm{d}W_{0}^{\intercal}\right)\right)
=tr⁡(W1​(∂ℒ∂M)⊺​d​W0)+tr⁡(WQ​WK⊺​W0⊺​(∂ℒ∂Φ)⊺​d​W0)+tr⁡(WK​WQ⊺​W0⊺​(∂ℒ∂Φ)​d​W0)\displaystyle=\operatorname{tr}\left(W_{1}\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}\right)^{\intercal}\mathrm{d}W_{0}\right)+\operatorname{tr}\left(W_{Q}W_{K}^{\intercal}W_{0}^{\intercal}\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}\right)^{\intercal}\mathrm{d}W_{0}\right)+\operatorname{tr}\left(W_{K}W_{Q}^{\intercal}W_{0}^{\intercal}\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}\right)\mathrm{d}W_{0}\right)
=⟨∂ℒ∂M​W1⊺+∂ℒ∂Φ​W0​WK​WQ⊺+(∂ℒ∂Φ)⊺​W0​WQ​WK⊺,d​W0⟩\displaystyle=\left\langle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}W_{1}^{\intercal}+\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}W_{0}W_{K}W_{Q}^{\intercal}+\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}\right)^{\intercal}W_{0}W_{Q}W_{K}^{\intercal},\mathrm{d}W_{0}\right\rangle

Therefore, we obtain an expression for ∂ℒ∂W0\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial W_{0}}. Since we are considering gradient descent, the evolution of the parameters follows the direction of the negative gradient. Then we derive the expression of ∂ℒ∂M\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M} and ∂ℒ∂Φ\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi} in large NN and ss limit. Taking the total differential of the loss and taking the term about d​M\mathrm{d}M, we get

Proof of Lemma 3.1
Proof.

Let Δ​θ​(t):=θ⁡(t)−θ∗\Delta\theta(t):=\theta(t)-\theta_{*}. Since F⁡(θ∗)=0F(\theta_{*})=0 and J=D​F​(θ∗)J=DF(\theta_{*}), we can write

Δ˙​θ​(t)=J​Δ​θ​(t)+R⁡(Δ​θ​(t)),R⁡(Δ​θ):=F⁡(θ∗+Δ​θ)−J​Δ​θ.\dot{\Delta}\theta(t)=J\Delta\theta(t)+R(\Delta\theta(t)),\qquad R(\Delta\theta):=F(\theta_{*}+\Delta\theta)-J\Delta\theta. (42)

By assumption (6), for all ‖Δ​θ‖≤r\|\Delta\theta\|\leq r,

‖R⁡(Δ​θ)‖≤L​‖Δ​θ‖2.\|R(\Delta\theta)\|\leq L\|\Delta\theta\|^{2}. (43)
Step 1: Variation-of-constants representation.

Let Δ~​θ​(t):=eJ​t​Δ​θ​(0)\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t):=\mathrm{e}^{Jt}\Delta\theta(0) be the solution of the linearized system. From (42), the solution satisfies the Duhamel formula

Δ​θ​(t)=eJ​t​Δ​θ​(0)+∫0teJ⁡(t−s)​R​(Δ​θ​(s))​𝑑s=Δ~​θ​(t)+∫0teJ⁡(t−s)​R​(Δ​θ​(s))​𝑑s.\Delta\theta(t)=\mathrm{e}^{Jt}\Delta\theta(0)+\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{J(t-s)}R(\Delta\theta(s))\mathrm{d}s=\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)+\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{J(t-s)}R(\Delta\theta(s))\mathrm{d}s. (44)

Define the linearization error E⁡(t):=Δ​θ​(t)−Δ~​θ​(t)E(t):=\Delta\theta(t)-\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t). Then E⁡(0)=0E(0)=0 and by (44),

E⁡(t)=∫0teJ⁡(t−s)​R​(Δ​θ​(s))​𝑑s.E(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{J(t-s)}R(\Delta\theta(s))\mathrm{d}s. (45)
Step 2: A standard bound on the semigroup eJ​t\mathrm{e}^{Jt}.

Let μ:=sup{ℜ⁡(λ):λ∈σ⁡(J)}\mu:=\sup\{\Re(\lambda):\lambda\in\sigma(J)\}. In finite dimension, for the chosen operator norm there exists a constant K≥1K\geq 1 such that

‖eJ​t‖≤K​eμ​t,∀t≥0.\|\mathrm{e}^{Jt}\|\leq K\mathrm{e}^{\mu t},\qquad\forall t\geq 0. (46)
Step 3: Bootstrap control inside the neighborhood.

Fix a time horizon T>0T>0 such that

‖Δ~​θ​(t)‖≤r2,∀t∈[0,T].\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|\leq\frac{r}{2},\qquad\forall t\in[0,T]. (47)

We will show that for ε:=‖Δ​θ​(0)‖\varepsilon:=\|\Delta\theta(0)\| sufficiently small (depending on J,L,rJ,L,r), the trajectory stays in the ball ‖Δ​θ​(t)‖≤r\|\Delta\theta(t)\|\leq r on [0,T][0,T], so that (43) applies.

Indeed, from (44), (46), and (43), as long as ‖Δ​θ​(s)‖≤r\|\Delta\theta(s)\|\leq r for all s∈[0,t]s\in[0,t], we have

‖E⁡(t)‖≤∫0t‖eJ⁡(t−s)‖|R⁡(Δ​θ​(s))|𝑑s≤K​L​∫0teμ⁡(t−s)​‖Δ​θ​(s)‖2​𝑑s.\|E(t)\|\leq\int_{0}^{t}\|\mathrm{e}^{J(t-s)}\|\,\|R(\Delta\theta(s))\|\mathrm{d}s\leq KL\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{\mu(t-s)}\|\Delta\theta(s)\|^{2}\mathrm{d}s. (48)

Also ‖Δ~​θ​(t)‖≤‖eJ​t‖​‖Δ​θ​(0)‖≤K​ε​eμ​t\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|\leq\|\mathrm{e}^{Jt}\|\,\|\Delta\theta(0)\|\leq K\varepsilon\mathrm{e}^{\mu t}.

We now bootstrap the bound

‖Δ​θ​(t)‖≤2​‖Δ~​θ​(t)‖for all ​t∈[0,T].\|\Delta\theta(t)\|\leq 2\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|\quad\text{for all }t\in[0,T]. (49)

Assuming (49) holds on [0,t][0,t], then ‖Δ​θ​(s)‖≤2​‖Δ~​θ​(s)‖≤r\|\Delta\theta(s)\|\leq 2\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(s)\|\leq r by (47), so (48) applies and yields

‖E⁡(t)‖\displaystyle\|E(t)\| ≤K​L​∫0teμ⁡(t−s)​(2​‖Δ~​θ​(s)‖)2​𝑑s=4​K​L​∫0teμ⁡(t−s)​‖Δ~​θ​(s)‖2​𝑑s\displaystyle\leq KL\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{\mu(t-s)}\big(2\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(s)\|\big)^{2}\mathrm{d}s=4KL\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{\mu(t-s)}\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(s)\|^{2}\mathrm{d}s
≤4​K​L​∫0teμ⁡(t−s)​(K​ε​eμ​s)2​𝑑s=4​K3​L​ε2​eμ​t​∫0teμ​s​𝑑s.\displaystyle\leq 4KL\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{\mu(t-s)}\big(K\varepsilon\mathrm{e}^{\mu s}\big)^{2}\mathrm{d}s=4K^{3}L\,\varepsilon^{2}\,\mathrm{e}^{\mu t}\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{\mu s}\mathrm{d}s. (50)

If μ>0\mu>0, then ∫0teμ​s​𝑑s=(eμ​t−1)/μ≤eμ​t/μ\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{\mu s}ds=(\mathrm{e}^{\mu t}-1)/\mu\leq\mathrm{e}^{\mu t}/\mu, and thus

‖E⁡(t)‖≤4​K3​Lμ​ε2​e2​μ​t.\|E(t)\|\leq\frac{4K^{3}L}{\mu}\,\varepsilon^{2}\,\mathrm{e}^{2\mu t}. (51)

If μ=0\mu=0, then ∫0teμ​s​𝑑s=t\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{\mu s}ds=t and (50) gives

‖E⁡(t)‖≤4​K3​L​ε2​t.\|E(t)\|\leq 4K^{3}L\,\varepsilon^{2}\,t. (52)

(For μ<0\mu<0, one may similarly bound the integral by a constant and obtain a uniform O⁡(ε2)O(\varepsilon^{2}) error.)

Now choose ε\varepsilon small enough such that on [0,T][0,T],

‖E⁡(t)‖≤‖Δ~​θ​(t)‖∀t∈[0,T].\|E(t)\|\leq\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|\quad\forall t\in[0,T]. (53)

This is possible because by (47) we have ‖Δ~​θ​(t)‖≤r/2\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|\leq r/2, while (51) shows ‖E⁡(t)‖\|E(t)\| is O⁡(ε2)O(\varepsilon^{2}) times an exponential factor; e.g. it suffices to require

4​K3​Lμ​ε​eμ​T≤12(μ>0),or4​K3​L​ε​T≤12(μ=0),\frac{4K^{3}L}{\mu}\,\varepsilon\,\mathrm{e}^{\mu T}\leq\frac{1}{2}\quad(\mu>0),\qquad\text{or}\qquad 4K^{3}L\,\varepsilon\,T\leq\frac{1}{2}\quad(\mu=0),

and recall TT is such that ‖Δ~​θ​(t)‖≤r/2\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|\leq r/2 on [0,T][0,T], hence eμ​T\mathrm{e}^{\mu T} is at most on the order of 1/ε1/\varepsilon when μ>0\mu>0. Under (53),

‖Δ​θ​(t)‖≤‖Δ~​θ​(t)‖+‖E⁡(t)‖≤2|Δ~​θ​(t)|≤r,\|\Delta\theta(t)\|\leq\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|+\|E(t)\|\leq 2\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|\leq r,

so the bootstrap is self-consistent and (51) (or (52)) holds for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. This proves (7) with C=4​K3​LμC=\frac{4K^{3}L}{\mu} for μ>0\mu>0 and C=4​K3​LC=4K^{3}L for μ=0\mu=0.

Step 4: The Θ⁡(log⁡(1/ε))\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)) window when μ>0\mu>0.

If μ>0\mu>0, then ‖Δ~​θ​(t)‖≤K​ε​eμ​t\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|\leq K\varepsilon\mathrm{e}^{\mu t}. Therefore the condition ‖Δ~​θ​(t)‖≤r/2\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|\leq r/2 holds at least up to times

t≤1μ​log⁡r2​K​ε=Θ⁡(log⁡(1/ε)),t\leq\frac{1}{\mu}\log\frac{r}{2K\varepsilon}=\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)),

which is exactly the linearization window claimed in the lemma.

Step 5: Alignment with the unstable eigenvector with positive spectral gap.

Assume now that JJ has a simple eigenvalue μ>0\mu>0 with eigenvector vuv_{u} and a spectral gap: ℜ⁡(λ)≤μ−δ\Re(\lambda)\leq\mu-\delta for all other eigenvalues. Let Πu\Pi_{u} be the spectral projection onto span​{vu}\mathrm{span}\{v_{u}\} and Πs=I−Πu\Pi_{s}=I-\Pi_{u}. Then there exist constants Ku,KsK_{u},K_{s} such that

‖Πu​eJ​t‖≤Ku​eμ​t,‖Πs​eJ​t‖≤Ks​e(μ−δ)​t,∀t≥0.\|\Pi_{u}\mathrm{e}^{Jt}\|\leq K_{u}\mathrm{e}^{\mu t},\qquad\|\Pi_{s}\mathrm{e}^{Jt}\|\leq K_{s}\mathrm{e}^{(\mu-\delta)t},\qquad\forall t\geq 0. (54)

Write Δ~​θ​(t)=Πu​Δ~​θ​(t)+Πs​Δ~​θ​(t)\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)=\Pi_{u}\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)+\Pi_{s}\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t). If ⟨Δ⁡(0),vu⟩≠0\langle\Delta(0),v_{u}\rangle\neq 0, then Πu​Δ~​θ​(t)=a0​eμ​t​vu\Pi_{u}\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)=a_{0}\mathrm{e}^{\mu t}v_{u} for some a0≠0a_{0}\neq 0, while

‖Πs​Δ~​θ​(t)‖≤Ks​ε​e(μ−δ)​t.\|\Pi_{s}\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|\leq K_{s}\varepsilon\mathrm{e}^{(\mu-\delta)t}.

Hence

Δ~​θ​(t)‖Δ~​θ​(t)‖→±vu‖vu‖as ​t→∞,\frac{\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)}{\|\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|}\to\pm\frac{v_{u}}{\|v_{u}\|}\quad\text{as }t\to\infty, (55)

and the convergence rate is O⁡(e−δ​t)O(\mathrm{e}^{-\delta t}).

For the nonlinear trajectory, decompose Δ​θ​(t)=u⁡(t)+s⁡(t)\Delta\theta(t)=u(t)+s(t) with u⁡(t):=Πu​Δ​θ​(t)u(t):=\Pi_{u}\Delta\theta(t) and s⁡(t):=Πs​Δ​θ​(t)s(t):=\Pi_{s}\Delta\theta(t). Projecting (44) onto the two subspaces and using (54) gives

u⁡(t)=Πu​Δ~​θ​(t)+∫0tΠu​eJ⁡(t−s)​R​(Δ​θ​(s))​𝑑s,s⁡(t)=Πs​Δ~​θ​(t)+∫0tΠs​eJ⁡(t−s)​R​(Δ​θ​(s))​𝑑s.u(t)=\Pi_{u}\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)+\int_{0}^{t}\Pi_{u}\mathrm{e}^{J(t-s)}R(\Delta\theta(s))\ \mathrm{d}s,\quad s(t)=\Pi_{s}\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)+\int_{0}^{t}\Pi_{s}\mathrm{e}^{J(t-s)}R(\Delta\theta(s))\ \mathrm{d}s. (56)

Inside the linearization window we have ‖Δ​θ​(s)‖≤r\|\Delta\theta(s)\|\leq r, so (43) applies and, using also ‖Δ​θ​(s)‖≲ε​eμ​s\|\Delta\theta(s)\|\lesssim\varepsilon\mathrm{e}^{\mu s} from the bootstrap in Step 3, we obtain

‖R⁡(Δ⁡(s))‖≤L​‖Δ​θ​(s)‖2≲L​ε2​e2​μ​s.\|R(\Delta(s))\|\leq L\|\Delta\theta(s)\|^{2}\;\lesssim\;L\varepsilon^{2}\mathrm{e}^{2\mu s}.

Plugging into (56) yields, for tt in the linearization window,

‖u⁡(t)−Πu​Δ~​θ​(t)‖\displaystyle\|u(t)-\Pi_{u}\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\| ≤∫0t‖Πu​eJ⁡(t−s)‖​‖R⁡(Δ​θ​(s))‖​𝑑s≲ε2​e2​μ​t,\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{t}\|\Pi_{u}\mathrm{e}^{J(t-s)}\|\,\|R(\Delta\theta(s))\|\mathrm{d}s\;\lesssim\;\varepsilon^{2}\mathrm{e}^{2\mu t}, (57)
‖s⁡(t)−Πs​Δ~​θ​(t)‖\displaystyle\|s(t)-\Pi_{s}\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\| ≤∫0t‖Πs​eJ⁡(t−s)‖​‖R⁡(Δ​θ​(s))‖​𝑑s≲ε2​e2​μ​t.\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{t}\|\Pi_{s}\mathrm{e}^{J(t-s)}\|\,\|R(\Delta\theta(s))\|\mathrm{d}s\;\lesssim\;\varepsilon^{2}\mathrm{e}^{2\mu t}. (58)

Therefore,

‖s⁡(t)‖≤‖Πs​Δ~​θ​(t)‖+|s⁡(t)−Πs​Δ~​θ​(t)|≲ε​e(μ−δ)​t+ε2​e2​μ​t,\|s(t)\|\leq\|\Pi_{s}\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|+\|s(t)-\Pi_{s}\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|\;\lesssim\;\varepsilon\mathrm{e}^{(\mu-\delta)t}+\varepsilon^{2}\mathrm{e}^{2\mu t},

while

‖u⁡(t)‖≥‖Πu​Δ~​θ​(t)‖−|u⁡(t)−Πu​Δ~​θ​(t)|≳ε​eμ​t−ε2​e2​μ​t.\|u(t)\|\geq\|\Pi_{u}\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|-\|u(t)-\Pi_{u}\tilde{\Delta}\theta(t)\|\;\gtrsim\;\varepsilon\mathrm{e}^{\mu t}-\varepsilon^{2}\mathrm{e}^{2\mu t}.

Hence, for times tt such that ε​eμ​t\varepsilon\mathrm{e}^{\mu t} is still sufficiently small (which holds throughout a Θ⁡(log⁡(1/ε))\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)) interval inside the linearization window), we have

‖s⁡(t)‖‖u⁡(t)‖≲e−δ​t+ε​eμ​t.\frac{\|s(t)\|}{\|u(t)\|}\;\lesssim\;\mathrm{e}^{-\delta t}+\varepsilon\mathrm{e}^{\mu t}. (59)

Now let tt increase while remaining in the linearization window (so t→∞t\to\infty is possible as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0), and choose any sequence t=t⁡(ε)t=t(\varepsilon) such that

t(ε)→∞,εeμ​t​(ε)→0(e.g. t(ε)=12​μlog(1/ε)).t(\varepsilon)\to\infty,\qquad\varepsilon\mathrm{e}^{\mu t(\varepsilon)}\to 0\quad(\text{e.g. }t(\varepsilon)=\tfrac{1}{2\mu}\log(1/\varepsilon)).

Then (59) implies ‖s⁡(t)‖/‖u⁡(t)‖→0\|s(t)\|/\|u(t)\|\to 0, so

Δ​θ​(t)‖Δ​θ​(t)‖=u⁡(t)+s⁡(t)‖u⁡(t)+s⁡(t)‖→±vu‖vu‖.\frac{\Delta\theta(t)}{\|\Delta\theta(t)\|}=\frac{u(t)+s(t)}{\|u(t)+s(t)\|}\to\pm\frac{v_{u}}{\|v_{u}\|}.

This proves (8). ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.2
Proof.

The claim follows by a direct evaluation of the gradients at the origin. By Lemma 3.1, the early-time dynamics is governed by the linearization at θ=0\theta=0, so we substitute θ=0\theta=0 into (5).

At θ=0\theta=0, the definitions of 𝔸i\mathbb{A}_{i} and ℙi\mathbb{P}_{i} yield

𝔸i=π⊺,ℙi=1d𝟏⊺,for all i.\mathbb{A}_{i}=\pi^{\intercal},\qquad\mathbb{P}_{i}=\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}^{\intercal},\quad\text{for all }i.

Moreover, since π⊺\pi^{\intercal} is stationary, we have π⊺​P=π⊺\pi^{\intercal}P=\pi^{\intercal}, and hence

∑iπi​Pi=π⊺.\sum_{i}\pi_{i}P_{i}\;=\;\pi^{\intercal}.

Plugging these identities into the expression of ∂ℒ∂M\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M} in (5), we obtain

∂ℒ∂M|θ=0=−π​(π−1d​𝟏)⊺.\left.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}\right|_{\theta=0}=-\,\pi\left(\pi-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}\right)^{\intercal}.

This is exactly the desired formula, completing the proof. ∎

Analysis of transition between stage I and II

Although linearization reveals the characteristics of the first stage, gaps remain in the transition from the first to the second stage. At this point, simple linearization provides an error estimate that is too loose to accurately represent the stage transition. Therefore, a more refined error estimate is needed. To achieve this, we extend the techniques in (Chen et al., 2024c) or (Xu et al., 2025a) and prove a rigorous stage transition. Without loss of generality, we assume π⊺‖π‖​W0,W1​π−1d​𝟏‖π−1d​𝟏‖∼Θ⁡(ε)\frac{\pi^{\intercal}}{\|\pi\|}W_{0},W_{1}\frac{\pi-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}}{\|\pi-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}\|}\sim\Theta(\varepsilon). First, we introduce two quantities to show the magnitudes that distinguish the outer and inner parameters:

Wout, max=max⁡{‖W0‖F,‖W1‖F},Win, max=max⁡{‖WQ‖F,‖WK‖F}.W_{\text{out, max}}=\max\left\{\|W_{0}\|_{\mathrm{F}},\|W_{1}\|_{\mathrm{F}}\right\},\quad W_{\text{in, max}}=\max\left\{\|W_{Q}\|_{\mathrm{F}},\|W_{K}\|_{\mathrm{F}}\right\}. (60)

Then, recalling the definition of dynamics (4), we have the estimate of error term in transition of stage I and stage II:

‖∂ℒ∂Φ​W0​WQ​K⊺‖,‖(∂ℒ∂Φ)⊺​W0​WQ​K‖≲Wout, max3​Win, max2,\left\|\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}W_{0}W_{QK}^{\intercal}\right\|,\left\|\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}\right)^{\intercal}W_{0}W_{QK}\right\|\lesssim W_{\text{out, max}}^{3}W_{\text{in, max}}^{2}, (61)

and

‖W0⊺​∂ℒ∂Φ​W0​WK‖,‖W0⊺​(∂ℒ∂Φ)⊺​W0​WQ‖≲Wout, max4​Win, max.\left\|W_{0}^{\intercal}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}W_{0}W_{K}\right\|,\left\|W_{0}^{\intercal}\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}\right)^{\intercal}W_{0}W_{Q}\right\|\lesssim W_{\text{out, max}}^{4}W_{\text{in, max}}. (62)

Moreover, we decompose W0,W1W_{0},W_{1} into condensation directions and normal directions:

W0=π‖π‖​π⊺‖π‖​W0+R0,W1=W1​π−1d​𝟏‖π−1d​𝟏‖​π⊺−1d​𝟏⊺‖π−1d​𝟏‖+R1.W_{0}=\frac{\pi}{\|\pi\|}\frac{\pi^{\intercal}}{\|\pi\|}W_{0}+R_{0},\quad W_{1}=W_{1}\frac{\pi-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}}{\|\pi-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}\|}\frac{\pi^{\intercal}-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}^{\intercal}}{\|\pi-\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}\|}+R_{1}. (63)

where ℙj=exp⁡(π⊺​M​ej)∑j′exp⁡(π⊺​M​ej′)\mathbb{P}_{j}=\frac{\exp(\pi^{\intercal}Me_{j})}{\sum_{j^{\prime}}\exp(\pi^{\intercal}Me_{j^{\prime}})} and ‖E1‖≲Wout, max2​Win, max2\|E_{1}\|\lesssim W_{\text{out, max}}^{2}W_{\text{in, max}}^{2}. After establish the error estimate of the normal terms, We formally begin the proof of the phase transition. We divide the entire phase transition into two parts. The first part can be seen as a plateau period, where the condensation direction grows significantly and is about to become O⁡(1)O(1), while the normal direction remains small due to our fine error estimation. In the second part, the condensation direction rapidly reaches the neighborhood of the critical point.

We define

T1=sup{t≥0|Wout,max≲ε1n}T_{1}=\sup\left\{t\geq 0\ |\ W_{\text{out,max}}\lesssim\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{n}}\right\} (74)

Lemma C.1 (Refined error estimate).

For every t≤min⁡{T1,Tp}t\leq\min\{T_{1},T_{p}\}, one has

provided the initialization satisfies ‖WQ​(0)‖F+‖WK​(0)‖F+‖R0​(0)‖F+‖R1​(0)‖F≲ε\|W_{Q}(0)\|_{\mathrm{F}}+\|W_{K}(0)\|_{\mathrm{F}}+\|R_{0}(0)\|_{\mathrm{F}}+\|R_{1}(0)\|_{\mathrm{F}}\lesssim\varepsilon and ε>0\varepsilon>0 is sufficiently small.

Proof.

We start from the equations

d​WQd​t=−W0⊺​∂ℒ∂Φ​W0​WK,d​WKd​t=−W0⊺​(∂ℒ∂Φ)⊺​W0​WQ.\frac{dW_{Q}}{dt}=-W_{0}^{\intercal}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}W_{0}W_{K},\qquad\frac{dW_{K}}{dt}=-W_{0}^{\intercal}\Bigl(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}\Bigr)^{\intercal}W_{0}W_{Q}.

Hence

dd​t​(‖WQ‖F+‖WK‖F)≤C​ε4n​(‖WQ‖F+‖WK‖F).\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\|W_{Q}\|_{\mathrm{F}}+\|W_{K}\|_{\mathrm{F}}\bigr)\leq C\varepsilon^{\frac{4}{n}}\bigl(\|W_{Q}\|_{\mathrm{F}}+\|W_{K}\|_{\mathrm{F}}\bigr).

By Gronwall’s inequality and the assumption on the initialization, (76) follows.

Next, recall the expansion

∂ℒ∂M=−π⁡(π⊺−psym)+π⁡(π⊺​R0​W1​u​u⊺+π⊺​q​q⊺​W0​R1)​Var⁡(psym)+E,\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}=-\pi(\pi^{\intercal}-p_{\mathrm{sym}})+\pi\Bigl(\pi^{\intercal}R_{0}\,W_{1}uu^{\intercal}+\pi^{\intercal}qq^{\intercal}W_{0}R_{1}\Bigr)\operatorname{Var}(p_{\mathrm{sym}})+E, (78)

where

‖E‖≤C⁡(Wout,max2​Win,max2+‖R0‖F2+‖R1‖F2).\|E\|\leq C\Bigl(W_{\mathrm{out,max}}^{2}W_{\mathrm{in,max}}^{2}+\|R_{0}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}+\|R_{1}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\Bigr). (79)

Projecting the W0W_{0}-equation to the orthogonal complement of qq, we obtain

Similarly, projecting the W1W_{1}-equation to the orthogonal complement of uu, we get

Using the key identities

and the fact that Var⁡(psym)\operatorname{Var}(p_{\mathrm{sym}}) acts as a scalar on the subspace {v:⟨v,𝟏⟩=⟨v,u⟩=0}\{v:\langle v,\mathbf{1}\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle=0\}, we obtain

Combining the two inequalities, using (76), and applying a standard bootstrap argument yields (77). ∎

Remark C.3.

At first glance, this proposition resembles the previous linearization result. However, the key distinction is that here we obtain a significantly stronger control of the dynamics in the normal directions. This stronger control is essential for carrying out the cross-stage analysis.

To complete the cross-stage analysis, we need a dynamics so that we can work with a significant condensation direction. Specifically, observing the Eq. (81), we find that

z˙=‖π‖​‖π−psym​(z)‖​(‖a‖2+‖b‖2)+⟨ℰa,b⟩+⟨ℰb,a⟩\dot{z}=\|\pi\|\,\|\pi-p_{\mathrm{sym}}(z)\|\,(\|a\|^{2}+\|b\|^{2})+\langle\mathcal{E}_{a},b\rangle+\langle\mathcal{E}_{b},a\rangle (87)

Thus, if can establish the conservation law in this case. we can get the dynamics of zz which is solvable. For given small δ\delta, we define

T3=sup{t≥0|Wout,max≲1}T_{3}=\sup\left\{t\geq 0\ |\ W_{\text{out,max}}\lesssim 1\right\} (89)

and give a estimate of T2,T3T_{2},T_{3} by

Then first we get similar error estimate, the proof is similar to Lemma C.1. Thus we omit its proof.

C.3 Theoretical details in Sec. 3.3

Proof of Proposition 3.6

We complete the proof of Proposition 1 in two steps. First, we directly verify that a rank-one manifold is an invariant manifold. Then, we utilize data symmetry and permutation equivariance to prove the conservation of low-frequency tokens.

Proof.

(i) Invariance of the rank-one form. Plug (18) into (4) and check that each right-hand side remains in the same rank-one span.

Since W1⊺=β​α1⊺W_{1}^{\intercal}=\beta\,\alpha_{1}^{\intercal},

which is of the form γ˙​α1⊺\dot{\gamma}\,\alpha_{1}^{\intercal}.

Therefore the Φ\Phi-driven terms in W˙0\dot{W}_{0} satisfy

so W˙0\dot{W}_{0} stays in the span of {⋅α1⊺}\{\cdot\,\alpha_{1}^{\intercal}\} and hence W0​(t)=γ⁡(t)​α1⊺W_{0}(t)=\gamma(t)\alpha_{1}^{\intercal}.

which is of the form α1​β˙⊺\alpha_{1}\,\dot{\beta}^{\intercal}.

Finally,

W˙Q=−W0⊺​∂ℒ∂Φ​W0​WK=−λK​(γ⊺​∂ℒ∂Φ​γ)​α1​α~1⊺,\dot{W}_{Q}=-\,W_{0}^{\intercal}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}W_{0}W_{K}=-\lambda_{K}\big(\gamma^{\intercal}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}\gamma\big)\,\alpha_{1}\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\intercal},

so WQW_{Q} remains in the form λQ​(t)​α1​α~1⊺\lambda_{Q}(t)\alpha_{1}\tilde{\alpha}_{1}^{\intercal}. The argument for WKW_{K} is identical. Thus the flow stays in 𝒲\mathcal{W}.

(ii) Preservation of the low-frequency symmetry. Let

G:={σ:{1,…,V}→{1,…,V}|σ(1)=1}.G:=\{\sigma:\{1,\dots,V\}\rightarrow\{1,\dots,V\}|\ \sigma(1)=1\}. (147)

and let σ∈G\sigma\in G be the permutation matrix. Define the group action as

Proof of Theorem 3.7

We proceed with the proof of Theorem 3.7. First, we introduce some notation to show that the dynamics on a rank-one manifold will be further simplified in the case of low-frequency symmetry. Next, since we are still near the critical point described in Proposition 1, this means that we are also near the critical point for the dynamics on a rank-one manifold. Therefore, we continue using linearization methods to obtain the key conservation law results.

First, we find that the proxy attention matrix 𝔸\mathbb{A} has the form on 𝒲\mathcal{W} by direct computation,

𝔸=(ξ11−ξ1|𝒱|−1⋯1−ξ1|𝒱|−1ξ21−ξ2|𝒱|−1⋯1−ξ2|𝒱|−1ξ21−ξ2|𝒱|−1⋯1−ξ2|𝒱|−1),\mathbb{A}=\begin{pmatrix}\xi_{1}&\frac{1-\xi_{1}}{|\mathcal{V}|-1}&\cdots&\frac{1-\xi_{1}}{|\mathcal{V}|-1}\\ \xi_{2}&\frac{1-\xi_{2}}{|\mathcal{V}|-1}&\cdots&\frac{1-\xi_{2}}{|\mathcal{V}|-1}\\ \vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\ \xi_{2}&\frac{1-\xi_{2}}{|\mathcal{V}|-1}&\cdots&\frac{1-\xi_{2}}{|\mathcal{V}|-1}\end{pmatrix},

where

ξ2\displaystyle\xi_{2} =π1​exp⁡(η​γ1​γi≠1)π1​exp⁡(η​γ1​γi≠1)+(1−π1)​exp⁡(η​γi≠12).\displaystyle=\frac{\pi_{1}\exp\big(\eta\gamma_{1}\gamma_{i\neq 1}\big)}{\pi_{1}\exp\big(\eta\gamma_{1}\gamma_{i\neq 1}\big)+(1-\pi_{1})\exp\big(\eta\gamma_{i\neq 1}^{2}\big)}. (150)

Define the row-wise scalar projections

m1:=𝔸1​γ,m2:=𝔸2​γ.m_{1}:=\mathbb{A}_{1}\gamma,\qquad m_{2}:=\mathbb{A}_{2}\gamma.

Then

m1=γi≠1+ξ1​Δ​γ,m2=γi≠1+ξ2​Δ​γ.m_{1}=\gamma_{i\neq 1}+\xi_{1}\Delta\gamma,\qquad m_{2}=\gamma_{i\neq 1}+\xi_{2}\Delta\gamma.

Since 𝔸i​M=(𝔸i​γ)​β⊺=mi​β⊺\mathbb{A}_{i}M=(\mathbb{A}_{i}\gamma)\beta^{\intercal}=m_{i}\beta^{\intercal}, the model probability of predicting the first token is

p^i:=ℙi,1=exp⁡(mi​β1)exp⁡(mi​β1)+(|𝒱|−1)​exp⁡(mi​βi≠1)=σ⁡(mi​Δ​β−log⁡(|𝒱|−1)),i∈{1,2},\hat{p}_{i}:=\mathbb{P}_{i,1}=\frac{\exp(m_{i}\beta_{1})}{\exp(m_{i}\beta_{1})+(|\mathcal{V}|-1)\exp(m_{i}\beta_{i\neq 1})}=\sigma\!\big(m_{i}\Delta\beta-\log(|\mathcal{V}|-1)\big),\qquad i\in\{1,2\}, (151)

where σ\sigma is the sigmoid function. Here, we only consider the first and second probability because ℙi,1=ℙj,1\mathbb{P}_{i,1}=\mathbb{P}_{j,1} for i,j≠1i,j\neq 1. Moreover, there exists a key term (Pi−ℙi)​β(P_{i}-\mathbb{P}_{i})\beta in the following computation. By direct computation,

(Pi−ℙi)​β\displaystyle(P_{i}-\mathbb{P}_{i})\beta =(Pi,1−ℙi,1)​β1+((1−Pi,1−(1−ℙi,1)))​βi≠1\displaystyle=(P_{i,1}-\mathbb{P}_{i,1})\beta_{1}+\left((1-P_{i,1}-(1-\mathbb{P}_{i,1}))\right)\beta_{i\neq 1} (152)

Appendix D Theoretical details in Sec. 3.4

This appendix provides detailed proofs for Section 4.4. We focus on the minimal vocabulary size d=3d=3 to exhibit the separation between secondary high frequency and secondary low frequency. Throughout, we use the rank-one parametrization on the invariant manifold (cf. Proposition 3.6)

M=γ​β⊺,Φ=η​γ​γ⊺,θ=(γ,β)∈ℝ3×ℝ3.M=\gamma\beta^{\intercal},\qquad\Phi=\eta\,\gamma\gamma^{\intercal},\qquad\theta=(\gamma,\beta)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}.

Here, we do not need to consider η\eta, because calculations show that its derivatives up to the second order are zero, so it will not affect our analysis.

D.1 A degenerate critical point on the rank-one manifold

We first formalize the “bad” critical point on the rank-one manifold under symmetric frequencies. This critical point is degenerate in the sense that the key driving terms ∂ℒ/∂M\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial M and ∂ℒ/∂Φ\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\Phi vanish, hence linearization on the manifold cannot explain the escape to new embedding directions. The following is the proof of Proposition 3.8.

Proof.

We construct a critical point on the rank-one manifold and show it is a local minimum for the linearized dynamics.

The critical point is constructed as follows. Take γ1​γi≠1<0\gamma_{1}\gamma_{i\neq 1}<0 as shown in Theorem 3.7. When η\eta is sufficiently large, the attention proxy satisfies 𝔸1≈e1\mathbb{A}_{1}\approx e_{1} and 𝔸i≠1≈e^1:=(0,12,12)\mathbb{A}_{i\neq 1}\approx\hat{e}_{1}:=(0,\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}). Choose β1>βi≠1\beta_{1}>\beta_{i\neq 1} so that softmax⁡(k​β⊺)→e1\operatorname{softmax}(k\beta^{\intercal})\to e_{1} as k→+∞k\to+\infty and softmax⁡(k​β⊺)→e^1\operatorname{softmax}(k\beta^{\intercal})\to\hat{e}_{1} as k→−∞k\to-\infty. Thus we may choose γ1>0\gamma_{1}>0 and γi≠1<0\gamma_{i\neq 1}<0 so that

ℙ1=P1,ℙi≠1=12​(P2+P3).\mathbb{P}_{1}=P_{1},\qquad\mathbb{P}_{i\neq 1}=\tfrac{1}{2}(P_{2}+P_{3}).

By direct computation and symmetry of the data, we have ∂ℒ∂M=0\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}=0 and ∂ℒ∂Φ=0\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}=0 at this point (refer to Lemma D.4). Substituting this fact into Eq. (4), it implies that our construction gives a critical point.

To verify local minimality for the linearized dynamics, we linearize the dynamics in Eq. (4). We compute d⁡(∂ℒ∂M)\mathrm{d}\big(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}\big) and d⁡(∂ℒ∂Φ)\mathrm{d}\big(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}\big). At the constructed symmetric point, Lemma D.5 implies ∑iπi​d​𝔸i⊺​(Pi−ℙi)=0\sum_{i}\pi_{i}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{A}_{i}^{\intercal}(P_{i}-\mathbb{P}_{i})=0 and hence

d​∂ℒ∂M=∑iπi​𝔸i⊺​d​ℙi≠0.\mathrm{d}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}=\sum_{i}\pi_{i}\mathbb{A}_{i}^{\intercal}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{i}\neq 0.

Moreover, Lemma D.5 shows that d​ℙi=𝔸i​d​M​Var⁡(ℙi)\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{i}=\mathbb{A}_{i}\,\mathrm{d}M\,\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{P}_{i}). Since 𝔸2=𝔸3\mathbb{A}_{2}=\mathbb{A}_{3}, it implies that d​ℙ2=d​ℙ3\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{2}=\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{3}. In addition, Lemma D.5 gives d⁡(∂ℒ/∂Φ)=0\mathrm{d}(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\Phi)=0.

As a result, the linearized dynamics on (γ,β,η)(\gamma,\beta,\eta) reduces to

d​Δ​γd​t=−d⁡(∂ℒ∂M)​β,d​Δ​βd​t=−d​(∂ℒ∂M)⊺​γ,d​Δ​ηd​t=0,\frac{\mathrm{d}\Delta\gamma}{\mathrm{d}t}=-\mathrm{d}\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}\right)\beta,\qquad\frac{\mathrm{d}\Delta\beta}{\mathrm{d}t}=-\mathrm{d}\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}\right)^{\intercal}\gamma,\qquad\frac{\mathrm{d}\Delta\eta}{\mathrm{d}t}=0, (160)

and the Jacobian J0=−∇θ2ℒJ_{0}=-\nabla_{\theta}^{2}\mathcal{L} admits the explicit block form in Lemma D.6. In particular, J0J_{0} is negative semidefinite with a nontrivial kernel. Hence, the critical point we constructed is a neutrally stable equilibrium for the linearized dynamics, which motivates the Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction in the main text. ∎

D.2 Breaking the degeneracy: frequency perturbation and Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction

To eliminate the degeneracy, we perturb the frequencies between the two low-frequency states:

π⊺=(c,1−c2,1−c2)⇒π~⊺=(c,1−c2+δ,1−c2−δ).\pi^{\intercal}=\Big(c,\frac{1-c}{2},\frac{1-c}{2}\Big)\quad\Rightarrow\quad\tilde{\pi}^{\intercal}=\Big(c,\frac{1-c}{2}+\delta,\frac{1-c}{2}-\delta\Big). (161)

The dynamics becomes

θ˙=−∇θℒ​(θ,δ).\dot{\theta}=-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta,\delta).

We study the perturbed critical point by solving

−∇θℒ​(θ,δ)=0-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta,\delta)=0 (162)

near the degenerate minimum, which we shift to θ=0\theta=0 for convenience.

We use the formal expansion (at θ=0\theta=0):

−∇θℒ​(θ,δ)=J0​θ+δ​f1+12​B​(θ,θ)+δ​J1​θ+12​δ2​f2+h.o.t.,-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta,\delta)=J_{0}\theta+\delta f_{1}+\frac{1}{2}B(\theta,\theta)+\delta J_{1}\theta+\frac{1}{2}\delta^{2}f_{2}+\text{h.o.t.}, (163)

where

J0=−∇θ2ℒ,f1=∂δ(−∇θℒ),B⁡(⋅,⋅)=−∇θ3ℒ,J1=∂δJ0,f2=∂δ2(−∇θℒ).J_{0}=-\nabla_{\theta}^{2}\mathcal{L},\quad f_{1}=\partial_{\delta}(-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}),\quad B(\cdot,\cdot)=-\nabla_{\theta}^{3}\mathcal{L},\quad J_{1}=\partial_{\delta}J_{0},\quad f_{2}=\partial_{\delta}^{2}(-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}).

Since J0J_{0} is singular, we apply Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction.

D.2.3 Reduced kernel equation and approximate critical point

Plugging y=ζ⁡(x,δ)y=\zeta(x,\delta) into the kernel equation gives

−QK⊺∇ℒ(QKx+QRζ(x,δ),δ)=0.-Q_{K}^{\intercal}\nabla\mathcal{L}(Q_{K}x+Q_{R}\zeta(x,\delta),\delta)=0.

Because J0​QK=0J_{0}Q_{K}=0 and QK⊺​f1=0Q_{K}^{\intercal}f_{1}=0, the leading contributions are second order:

QK⊺​(12​B​(θ,θ)+δ​J1​θ+12​δ2​f2)+h.o.t.=0,θ=QK​x+QR​ζ​(x,δ).Q_{K}^{\intercal}\Big(\frac{1}{2}B(\theta,\theta)+\delta J_{1}\theta+\frac{1}{2}\delta^{2}f_{2}\Big)+\text{h.o.t.}=0,\qquad\theta=Q_{K}x+Q_{R}\zeta(x,\delta).
Theorem D.3 (Existence of an approximate critical point and its two-scale stability).

Let ζ⁡(x,δ)\zeta(x,\delta) be given by Proposition D.2. Then x=0x=0 is an approximate solution of the reduced kernel equation up to second order, i.e.

‖∇θℒ​(QR​ζ​(0,δ),δ)‖=𝒪⁡(δ3).\big\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(Q_{R}\zeta(0,\delta),\delta)\big\|=\mathcal{O}(\delta^{3}).

Moreover, the linear stability splits into two scales:

  1. 1.

    Slow manifold directions (within the rank-one manifold): any positive eigenvalues created from the kernel directions are at most 𝒪⁡(δ2)\mathcal{O}(\delta^{2}).

  2. 2.

    Fast transverse directions (escaping the manifold): Under condition in Lem. D.17, there exists a transverse positive eigenvalue of order Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta).

Proof.

The estimate ‖∇ℒ‖=𝒪⁡(δ3)\|\nabla\mathcal{L}\|=\mathcal{O}(\delta^{3}) follows by inserting θ=QR​ζ​(0,δ)\theta=Q_{R}\zeta(0,\delta) into the kernel expansion and using the explicit expressions:

  1. (1).

    12​QK⊺​B​(q2​y2,q2​y2)\frac{1}{2}Q_{K}^{\intercal}B(q_{2}y_{2},q_{2}y_{2}) (From Lem. D.13):

    12​QK⊺​B​(q2​y2,q2​y2)=1‖γ‖2+‖β‖2​(00π1​γ12​ℙ1,2+(1−π1)​γ22​ℙi≠1,2)​y22.\frac{1}{2}Q_{K}^{\intercal}B(q_{2}y_{2},q_{2}y_{2})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\|\gamma\|^{2}+\|\beta\|^{2}}}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\\ \pi_{1}\gamma_{1}^{2}\mathbb{P}_{1,2}+(1-\pi_{1})\gamma_{2}^{2}\mathbb{P}_{i\neq 1,2}\end{pmatrix}y_{2}^{2}.
  2. (2).

    δ​QK⊺​J1​(q2​y2)\delta Q_{K}^{\intercal}J_{1}(q_{2}y_{2}) (From Lem. D.10):

    δ​QK⊺​J1​(q2​y2)=−δ​2‖γ‖2+‖β‖2​(00π1​γ1​(1−λ)+γi≠1​(λ+(1−π1)​(1−λ)))​y2.\delta Q_{K}^{\intercal}J_{1}(q_{2}y_{2})=-\delta\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{\|\gamma\|^{2}+\|\beta\|^{2}}}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\\ \pi_{1}\gamma_{1}(1-\lambda)+\gamma_{i\neq 1}(\lambda+(1-\pi_{1})(1-\lambda))\end{pmatrix}y_{2}.
  3. (3).

    δ2​f2\delta^{2}f_{2} vanishes (From Lem. D.14).

Substitute y2=2​λ​γi≠1+(1−λ)​(π1​γ1+(1−π1)​γi≠1)π1​γ12​ℙ1,2+(1−π1)​γi≠12​ℙi≠1,2​δy_{2}=\sqrt{2}\,\frac{\lambda\gamma_{i\neq 1}+(1-\lambda)(\pi_{1}\gamma_{1}+(1-\pi_{1})\gamma_{i\neq 1})}{\pi_{1}\gamma_{1}^{2}\mathbb{P}_{1,2}+(1-\pi_{1})\gamma_{i\neq 1}^{2}\mathbb{P}_{i\neq 1,2}}\delta. We found that the second-order terms cancel each other out automatically.

For stability, we write the perturbed Hessian at the approximate critical point as

∇θ2​ℒ​(θ,δ)=J0+δ​H1+𝒪⁡(δ2),H1:=−((0BB⊺0)+(000C))+J1,\nabla_{\theta}^{2}\mathcal{L}(\theta,\delta)=J_{0}+\delta H_{1}+\mathcal{O}(\delta^{2}),\qquad H_{1}:=-\Big(\begin{pmatrix}0&B\\ B^{\intercal}&0\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 0&C\end{pmatrix}\Big)+J_{1},

with (B,C)(B,C) computed from the second-order kernel reduction (see Lem. D.15).

We take the basis as Q=(QK,QR)Q=(Q_{K},Q_{R}):

where Λ=QR⊺​J0​QR\Lambda=Q_{R}^{\intercal}J_{0}Q_{R}, G=QK⊺​H1​QKG=Q_{K}^{\intercal}H_{1}Q_{K}, E=QK⊺​H1​QRE=Q_{K}^{\intercal}H_{1}Q_{R}, and F=QR⊺​H1​QRF=Q_{R}^{\intercal}H_{1}Q_{R}. Let λ\lambda be a small eigenvalue and the corresponding eigenvector is (x,y)(x,y), the equation is

{δ​G​x+δ​E​y+𝒪⁡(δ2)=λ​xΛ​y+δ​E⊺​x+𝒪⁡(δ)​y=λ​y\left\{\begin{aligned} \delta Gx+\delta Ey+\mathcal{O}(\delta^{2})&=\lambda x\\ \Lambda y+\delta E^{\intercal}x+\mathcal{O}(\delta)y&=\lambda y\end{aligned}\right. (171)

Substitute this expression into the the first equation, we get

{d​Δ​W0d​t=Δ⁡(−∂ℒ∂M​W1⊺−∂ℒ∂Φ​W0​WK​WQ⊺−(∂ℒ∂Φ)⊺​W0​WQ​WK⊺)d​Δ​W1d​t=Δ⁡(−W0⊺​∂ℒ∂M)d​Δ​WQd​t=Δ⁡(−W0⊺​∂ℒ∂Φ​W0​WK)d​Δ​WKd​t=Δ⁡(−W0⊺​(∂ℒ∂Φ)⊺​W0​WQ)\left\{\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d}\Delta W_{0}}{\mathrm{d}t}&=\Delta\left(-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}W_{1}^{\intercal}-\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}W_{0}W_{K}W_{Q}^{\intercal}-\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}\right)^{\intercal}W_{0}W_{Q}W_{K}^{\intercal}\right)\\ \frac{\mathrm{d}\Delta W_{1}}{\mathrm{d}t}&=\Delta\left(-W_{0}^{\intercal}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}\right)\\ \frac{\mathrm{d}\Delta W_{Q}}{\mathrm{d}t}&=\Delta\left(-W_{0}^{\intercal}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}W_{0}W_{K}\right)\\ \frac{\mathrm{d}\Delta W_{K}}{\mathrm{d}t}&=\Delta\left(-W_{0}^{\intercal}\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}\right)^{\intercal}W_{0}W_{Q}\right)\\ \end{aligned}\right. D.3.1 Vanishing of gradients

Lemma D.4 (∂ℒ/∂M=0\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial M=0 and ∂ℒ/∂Φ=0\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\Phi=0 at the constructed point).

At the symmetric degenerate minimum in Proposition 3.8, we have
