D.3.6 Computation of the bilinear form B⁡(⋅,⋅)B(\cdot,\cdot)

Before proceeding with the specific calculations, let’s review the following lemma.

Lemma D.11 (Second differential).

Let f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be C2C^{2}. Then for any h∈ℝdh\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

f⁡(θ+h)=f⁡(θ)+d​f​(θ)​[h]+12​d2​f​(θ)​[h,h]+𝒪⁡(‖h‖3),f(\theta+h)=f(\theta)+\mathrm{d}f(\theta)[h]+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{d}^{2}f(\theta)[h,h]+\mathcal{O}(\|h\|^{3}), (196)

where d2​f​(θ)​[u,v]=u⊺​∇2f​(θ)​v\mathrm{d}^{2}f(\theta)[u,v]=u^{\intercal}\nabla^{2}f(\theta)\,v is the (symmetric) bilinear form induced by the Hessian. The same expansion applies componentwise to vector-valued maps; in particular, for the gradient map g​(θ)=∇f​(θ)g(\theta)=\nabla f(\theta),

g⁡(θ+h)=g⁡(θ)+D​g​(θ)​h+12​D2​g​(θ)​[h,h]+𝒪⁡(‖h‖3).g(\theta+h)=g(\theta)+Dg(\theta)\,h+\frac{1}{2}\,D^{2}g(\theta)[h,h]+\mathcal{O}(\|h\|^{3}). (197)

Also, we have the following lemma which simplifies the computation.

Lemma D.12 (A useful identity: d​Var⁡(𝔸i≠1)=0\mathrm{d}\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{A}_{i\neq 1})=0 for the antisymmetric direction).

At 𝔸i≠1=e^1=(0,12,12)\mathbb{A}_{i\neq 1}=\hat{e}_{1}=(0,\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}), if d​𝔸i≠1=(0,a,−a)\mathrm{d}\mathbb{A}_{i\neq 1}=(0,a,-a) for some aa, then d​Var⁡(𝔸i≠1)=0\mathrm{d}\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{A}_{i\neq 1})=0.

Proof.

By definition, d​Var⁡(𝔸)=diag⁡(d​𝔸)−(d​𝔸)​𝔸⊺−𝔸​(d​𝔸)⊺\mathrm{d}\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{A})=\operatorname{diag}(\mathrm{d}\mathbb{A})-(\mathrm{d}\mathbb{A})\mathbb{A}^{\intercal}-\mathbb{A}(\mathrm{d}\mathbb{A})^{\intercal}. Substituting 𝔸=e^1\mathbb{A}=\hat{e}_{1} and d​𝔸=(0,a,−a)\mathrm{d}\mathbb{A}=(0,a,-a) gives exact cancellation of all entries. ∎

Consequently, in our regime the second differential of 𝔸i\mathbb{A}_{i} simplifies to

d2​𝔸i=d2​(η​γi​γ⊺)​Var⁡(𝔸i),\mathrm{d}^{2}\mathbb{A}_{i}=\mathrm{d}^{2}(\eta\,\gamma_{i}\gamma^{\intercal})\ \operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{A}_{i}), (198)

because the potentially present term d⁡(η​γi​γ⊺)​d​Var⁡(𝔸i)\mathrm{d}(\eta\gamma_{i}\gamma^{\intercal})\,\mathrm{d}\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{A}_{i}) vanishes (identically for i=1i=1 since d​𝔸1=0\mathrm{d}\mathbb{A}_{1}=0, and by Lemma D.12 for i≠1i\neq 1).

Recall

∂ℒ∂M=−∑iπi𝔸i⊺(Pi−ℙi).\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}=-\sum_{i}\pi_{i}\,\mathbb{A}_{i}^{\intercal}(P_{i}-\mathbb{P}_{i}). (199)

    −∑iπi∂δ2𝔸i⊺(Pi−ℙi)−2∑iπi∂δ𝔸i⊺∂δ(Pi−ℙi)−∑iπi𝔸i⊺∂δ2(Pi−ℙi)\displaystyle-\sum_{i}\pi_{i}\partial_{\delta}^{2}\mathbb{A}_{i}^{\intercal}(P_{i}-\mathbb{P}_{i})-2\sum_{i}\pi_{i}\partial_{\delta}\mathbb{A}_{i}^{\intercal}\partial_{\delta}(P_{i}-\mathbb{P}_{i})-\sum_{i}\pi_{i}\mathbb{A}_{i}^{\intercal}\partial_{\delta}^{2}(P_{i}-\mathbb{P}_{i})
    =−2∑i∂δπi∂δ𝔸i⊺(Pi−ℙi)−2∑i∂δπi𝔸i⊺∂δ(Pi−ℙi)−2∑iπi∂δ𝔸i⊺∂δ(Pi−ℙi)\displaystyle=-2\sum_{i}\partial_{\delta}\pi_{i}\partial_{\delta}\mathbb{A}_{i}^{\intercal}(P_{i}-\mathbb{P}_{i})-2\sum_{i}\partial_{\delta}\pi_{i}\mathbb{A}_{i}^{\intercal}\partial_{\delta}(P_{i}-\mathbb{P}_{i})-2\sum_{i}\pi_{i}\partial_{\delta}\mathbb{A}_{i}^{\intercal}\partial_{\delta}(P_{i}-\mathbb{P}_{i})

    −∑iπiei∂δ2(Pi−ℙi)M⊺Var(𝔸i)−2∑iπiei∂δ(Pi−ℙi)M⊺∂δVar(𝔸i)−∑iπiei(Pi−ℙi)M⊺∂δ2Var(𝔸i)\displaystyle-\sum_{i}\pi_{i}\,e_{i}\partial_{\delta}^{2}\big(P_{i}-\mathbb{P}_{i}\big)M^{\intercal}\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{A}_{i})-2\sum_{i}\pi_{i}\,e_{i}\partial_{\delta}\big(P_{i}-\mathbb{P}_{i}\big)M^{\intercal}\partial_{\delta}\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{A}_{i})-\sum_{i}\pi_{i}\,e_{i}\big(P_{i}-\mathbb{P}_{i}\big)M^{\intercal}\partial_{\delta}^{2}\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{A}_{i})

D.3.9 Fast transverse instability: Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta) eigenvalue

Lemma D.17 (A transverse eigenvalue of order Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta)).

Let c=λ​γi≠1+(1−λ)​(π1​γ1+(1−π1)​γi≠1)π1​γ12​ℙ1,2+(1−π1)​γi≠12​ℙi≠1,2c=\frac{\lambda\gamma_{i\neq 1}+(1-\lambda)(\pi_{1}\gamma_{1}+(1-\pi_{1})\gamma_{i\neq 1})}{\pi_{1}\gamma_{1}^{2}\mathbb{P}_{1,2}+(1-\pi_{1})\gamma_{i\neq 1}^{2}\mathbb{P}_{i\neq 1,2}} and assume that

c⁡(1−π1)​γi≠1​ℙi≠1,2−(λ+(1−π1)​(1−λ))≠0.c(1-\pi_{1})\gamma_{i\neq 1}\mathbb{P}_{i\neq 1,2}-(\lambda+(1-\pi_{1})(1-\lambda))\neq 0. (230)

At the perturbed point, ∂ℒ/∂Φ=𝒪⁡(δ2)\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\Phi=\mathcal{O}(\delta^{2}) while ∂ℒ/∂M=Θ⁡(δ)\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial M=\Theta(\delta). Consequently, linearizing the full dynamics (Eq. (174)) yields a transverse positive eigenvalue of size Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta).

Proof.

Since d​∂ℒ∂Φ=0\mathrm{d}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}=0 and ∂δ∂ℒ∂Φ=0\partial_{\delta}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}=0, we get ∂ℒ∂Φ=𝒪⁡(δ2)\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\Phi}=\mathcal{O}(\delta^{2}) after perturbation.

Next we compute perturbed ∂ℒ∂M\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M}. By Lemma D.5, we get the new term is

c​π1​γ1​(100)​(0,ℙ1,2,−ℙ1,2)+c⁡(1−π1)​γi≠1​(01212)​(0,ℙi≠1,2,−ℙi≠1,2)c\pi_{1}\gamma_{1}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right)\left(0,\mathbb{P}_{1,2},-\mathbb{P}_{1,2}\right)+c(1-\pi_{1})\gamma_{i\neq 1}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ \frac{1}{2}\\ \frac{1}{2}\end{array}\right)\left(0,\mathbb{P}_{i\neq 1,2},-\mathbb{P}_{i\neq 1,2}\right)

where c=λ​γi≠1+(1−λ)​(π1​γ1+(1−π1)​γi≠1)π1​γ12​ℙ1,2+(1−π1)​γi≠12​ℙi≠1,2​δc=\frac{\lambda\gamma_{i\neq 1}+(1-\lambda)(\pi_{1}\gamma_{1}+(1-\pi_{1})\gamma_{i\neq 1})}{\pi_{1}\gamma_{1}^{2}\mathbb{P}_{1,2}+(1-\pi_{1})\gamma_{i\neq 1}^{2}\mathbb{P}_{i\neq 1,2}}\delta.

However, from Eq. (186), we find that

∂∂δ​∂ℒ∂M\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\delta}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial M} =−(01212)​(0,λ,−λ)−(π112​(1−π1)12​(1−π1))​(0,1−λ,−(1−λ)).\displaystyle=-\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\[2.84526pt] \frac{1}{2}\\[2.84526pt] \frac{1}{2}\end{array}\right)(0,\lambda,-\lambda)-\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\pi_{1}\\ \frac{1}{2}(1-\pi_{1})\\ \frac{1}{2}(1-\pi_{1})\end{array}\right)(0,1-\lambda,-(1-\lambda)).

The two terms cannot cancel each other out by our assumption (A parameter that does not meet the condition is a zero test set), thus resulting in an Θ⁡(δ)\Theta(\delta) term. ∎

Appendix E Detailed Experiment Setup

E.1 Detailed Synthetic Experiment Setup

Dataset

To better induce an exponential decay in the stationary distribution, and to more clearly illustrate the phase transition, we adopt an exponentially decaying form

π0=(1/2, 1/4,…, 1/2d),π=π0/‖π0‖.\pi_{0}=\bigl(1/2,\;1/4,\;\ldots,\;1/2^{d}\bigr),\qquad\pi=\pi_{0}/\|\pi_{0}\|.

Following (Makkuva et al., 2025), diagonal dominant transition matrices are unfavorable local minima during optimization, we set λ=0.8\lambda=0.8 to ensure diagonal dominance. For a fixed sequence length of 2020, we sample 100,000100{,}000 sequences {Xi}i=1100,000\{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{100{,}000} from the resulting Markov chain, and use the last token Xi​[−1]X_{i}[-1] as the training label. By the Markov property, this label is completely determined by the second-to-last token Xi​[−2]X_{i}[-2]. Accordingly, we group both the training and test sets by the value of Xi​[−2]X_{i}[-2], denoting the group indexed by state kk as SkS_{k}.

Model

We follow exactly the model specification in Def. 2.2, with embedding dimension m=256m=256. Since our theoretical analysis is derived under small initialization, we adopt the initialization scheme of (Zhang et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2025b), initializing each weight independently as 𝒩⁡(0,1/m2)\mathcal{N}(0,1/m^{2}).

Training

We train the model using the Adam optimizer with a fixed learning rate of 1.5×10−41.5\times 10^{-4} and do not use any learning-rate scheduler.

E.2 Analysis Tools

Condensation Heatmap

To quantify parameter condensation, we compute the pairwise cosine similarity between the input-weight vectors of neurons in the weight matrix WW. Specifically, for the ii-th and jj-th neurons, we define

C(i,j)=W[i,:]⋅W[j,:]∥W[i,:]∥2∥W[j,:]∥2.C(i,j)=\frac{W[i,:]\cdot W[j,:]}{\|W[i,:]\|_{2}\,\|W[j,:]\|_{2}}.

For clearer visualization, we permute the rows and columns of the similarity matrix CC and display the reordered matrix in Fig. 2(A).

Embedding Visualization

Let W0,tW_{0,t} denote the embedding parameters at training epoch tt for t=0,…,Tt=0,\ldots,T. We form the collection of embedding snapshots {W0,0,…,W0,T}\{W_{0,0},\ldots,W_{0,T}\} and apply principal component analysis (PCA) to obtain the leading eigen-directions e^1\hat{e}_{1} and e^2\hat{e}_{2}. We then project the embedding vectors onto e^1\hat{e}_{1} and e^2\hat{e}_{2} to produce the two-dimensional visualization shown in Fig. 2(B).
